names.meaning: The LORD is my strength (Uzziah); The LORD has helped (Azariah)

events.title: Becomes king at sixteen
events.summary: Made king by the people after his father Amaziah; he reigned fifty-two years and did what was right, though the high places remained.

events.title: Prospers while seeking God under Zechariah
events.summary: Chronicles links his military success, building of towers and cisterns, and inventive siege engines to the period when he sought God under the instruction of Zechariah.

events.title: Burns incense in the temple and is struck with leprosy
events.summary: Grown proud, he entered the sanctuary to burn incense, a priestly task. Confronted by Azariah the priest and eighty others, he raged and was struck with a skin disease, living in a separate house while his son Jotham governed.

events.title: Death of King Uzziah
events.summary: He was buried in a field near the royal tombs because of his disease. Isaiah dates his temple vision to the year of Uzziah's death.

summary: Uzziah (also called Azariah) ruled Judah for fifty-two years in the eighth century BC, a long, prosperous reign that paralleled Jeroboam II in the north. Chronicles portrays a capable builder, farmer and soldier who expanded Judah's reach toward Edom and Philistia, but whose pride led him to usurp the priestly office of burning incense; he spent his last years with a skin disease while his son Jotham acted as regent. His death frames Isaiah's call, and the prophetic books of Hosea and Amos are dated by his reign.
textSays: Kings gives a brief, positive notice and records that the LORD struck him so that he was leprous until his death (2 Kgs 15:1-7). Chronicles adds his building and military projects and explains the disease as the result of his intrusion into the temple (2 Chr 26:16-21).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition links the earthquake of Amos 1:1 and Zech 14:5 to the moment Uzziah entered the sanctuary, making his sin a cosmic disturbance (Josephus, Antiquities 9.10.4, tells a similar story).

Often read as a warning that strength and success can breed pride, and as an illustration of the boundary between royal and priestly office later fulfilled in Christ, who is both king and priest (Heb 7:1-17).

context: Uzziah's reign fell in a lull of Assyrian pressure before Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BC), allowing both Israel and Judah to expand. A Second Temple-period stone plaque found on the Mount of Olives reads that the bones of Uzziah king of Judah were brought there, showing his remains were later reburied.
legacy: His death year became a fixed point in prophetic chronology (Isa 6:1), and the earthquake in his days was remembered for centuries (Zech 14:5).
voice: A confident, practical builder-king who speaks of towers, cisterns and engines, impatient with restraint, and in later years subdued and isolated.

alternatives.label: If accession was 729 BC at age 25
Accession or co-regency in Hoshea's third year (2 Kgs 18:1)

events.title: Cleanses and reopens the temple
events.summary: In his first month he opened the temple doors his father Ahaz had shut, had the Levites purify the house, and restored sacrifices and Levitical music.

events.title: Celebrates a national Passover
events.summary: He sent couriers through Judah and the remnant of the northern tribes inviting them to Passover; some mocked, but many came, and the feast was extended a second week.

events.title: Removes high places and breaks Nehushtan
events.summary: He destroyed the high places and pillars and broke in pieces the bronze serpent made by Moses, to which Israel had been burning incense.

events.title: Rebels against Assyria
events.summary: He refused to serve the king of Assyria and struck the Philistines as far as Gaza.

events.title: Prepares Jerusalem for siege
events.summary: He blocked springs outside the city, rebuilt the wall, and channelled the waters of Gihon down to the west side of the City of David, the work usually identified with the Siloam tunnel.

events.title: Sennacherib invades; Hezekiah pays tribute
events.summary: Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah, at Lachish's fall, sent silver and gold stripped even from the temple doors.

events.title: The Rabshakeh's speech and Hezekiah's prayer
events.summary: An Assyrian officer mocked Hezekiah's trust in the LORD before the walls. Hezekiah tore his clothes, sent to Isaiah, and spread the Assyrian letter before the LORD in the temple.

events.title: Jerusalem delivered
events.summary: Isaiah announced that the Assyrian would not enter the city; the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh.

events.title: Illness and fifteen added years
events.summary: Told to set his house in order, he wept and prayed; Isaiah returned with a promise of fifteen more years, confirmed by the shadow going back on the steps of Ahaz.

events.title: Shows his treasures to Babylonian envoys
events.summary: He displayed his storehouses to envoys of Merodach-baladan; Isaiah foretold that all of it would be carried to Babylon. Hezekiah answered that at least there would be peace in his own days.

events.title: Death and burial
events.summary: He died honoured by all Judah and was succeeded by his son Manasseh.

summary:
Hezekiah son of Ahaz was king of Judah at the turning point of the Assyrian age. Inheriting a kingdom that his father had made an Assyrian vassal and whose temple had been closed, he reopened and purified the temple, held a Passover to which he invited the survivors of the fallen northern kingdom, and removed local shrines and even Moses' bronze serpent. Kings says there was none like him among the kings of Judah in trusting the LORD.

His reign is also one of the best-attested in the ancient Near East. He prepared Jerusalem for war, cutting the water tunnel that still runs under the City of David, and in 701 BC faced Sennacherib's invasion. Assyrian annals boast of shutting him up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage' and receiving heavy tribute; the biblical account agrees on the tribute but climaxes in the city's deliverance after Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's oracle.

The narrative does not idealise him. After his recovery from a mortal illness, he proudly showed Babylonian envoys his treasures and received Isaiah's announcement of future exile with relief that it would not come in his own lifetime. He is remembered as a model of reforming, praying kingship who nevertheless left a son, Manasseh, who undid his reforms.
textSays: Kings, Chronicles and Isaiah each narrate his reign (2 Kgs 18:1-20:21; 2 Chr 29:1-32:33; Isa 36:1-39:8). The text states he trusted the LORD and held fast to him (2 Kgs 18:5-6), rebelled against Assyria (2 Kgs 18:7), paid tribute to Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:14-16), prayed for deliverance (2 Kgs 19:15-19), was granted fifteen more years (2 Kgs 20:6), and was rebuked for his display to Babylon (2 Kgs 20:16-18). Chronicles adds his temple restoration and Passover and notes that God left him to test him (2 Chr 32:31). Proverbs credits his men with copying proverbs of Solomon (Prov 25:1).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition praises Hezekiah as a king who spread Torah study throughout the land, and the Talmud credits 'Hezekiah and his company' with writing down Isaiah, Proverbs, Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (b. Bava Batra 15a). Some sages said he could have been the Messiah but failed to sing praise after his deliverance (b. Sanhedrin 94a).
Read as a type of faithful prayer and reform; his song in Isa 38:10-20 is used as a canticle in the Liturgy of the Hours (Lauds), and he appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:9-10).

Frequently held up as the model reformer who restores pure worship according to the word, even destroying a venerable relic (the bronze serpent) when it became an object of misplaced devotion; his response to Isaiah's oracle is read as a caution about short-sighted faith.

Many scholars see the account as shaped by later Deuteronomistic editors who made Hezekiah a forerunner of Josiah. Debate continues over whether 2 Kgs 18:13-16 and 18:17-19:37 preserve one campaign or two, and over the internal chronology (2 Kgs 18:1 versus 18:13).

strengths: Restored temple worship immediately on accession
Trusted God and prayed under overwhelming threat
Practical and far-sighted preparations for siege
Humbled himself when confronted (2 Chr 32:26)
failures: Rebelled against Assyria in alliance-seeking that Isaiah criticised (Isa 30:1-5)
Displayed his treasures to Babylon and was complacent about the coming exile
turningPoints: Opening the temple in his first month

context: Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC, early in or just before his reign, leaving Judah alone between Assyria and Egypt. Archaeology supplies unusual corroboration: Sennacherib's annals (Taylor and Oriental Institute prisms), the Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, the Siloam tunnel inscription, the Broad Wall in Jerusalem, thousands of royal (lmlk) storage-jar handles, and a clay seal impression reading 'Belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah' found on the Ophel in 2009 and published in 2015.
legacy: Hezekiah became the standard of the trusting reformer-king alongside Josiah (2 Kgs 18:5; 2 Kgs 23:25). Jeremiah's contemporaries remembered that he heeded Micah's warning (Jer 26:18-19), and Ben Sira praises him for fortifying the city and bringing water into it (Sirach 48:17-22).

traditions.text: Hezekiah and his circle are credited with writing down (editing) Isaiah, Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes.
Hezekiah is said to have hidden away a 'book of remedies' so that people would pray rather than rely on it, an act the sages approved.

voice: Earnest and devout, quick to tear his clothes and pray aloud, but also a shrewd planner who talks of tunnels, walls and storehouses; under praise he can slip into self-satisfaction.

skills.name: Building and fortification after his restoration

events.title: Becomes king at twelve and rebuilds the high places
events.summary: He reigned fifty-five years, the longest of any king of Judah. He rebuilt the high places, raised altars to Baal and the host of heaven in the temple courts, practised divination, and made his son pass through the fire.

events.title: Sheds much innocent blood
events.summary: Kings says he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and later names his sins as the reason judgment on Judah could not be averted.

events.title: Taken to Babylon in chains and repents
events.summary: Chronicles alone reports that Assyrian commanders took him with hooks to Babylon, where he humbled himself and prayed; God restored him to Jerusalem.

events.title: Partial reform after restoration
events.summary: He fortified Jerusalem, removed foreign gods from the temple and restored the altar of the LORD, though the people still sacrificed at high places.

summary: Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, reigned fifty-five years in the seventh century BC as a loyal vassal of Assyria. Kings presents him as the worst king of Judah, reversing his father's reforms, introducing astral and Canaanite cults into the temple, sacrificing his son, and shedding innocent blood, so that his reign becomes the stated reason for the exile. Chronicles adds a striking twist: taken captive to Babylon, he repented, prayed, and was restored, becoming a picture of grace for the worst of sinners.
textSays: 2 Kgs 21:1-18 records only his apostasy and violence and later blames the exile on his sins (2 Kgs 23:26; 2 Kgs 24:3-4; Jer 15:4). 2 Chr 33:1-20 records the same sins but adds his captivity, repentance and partial reform.

interpretations.view: The Mishnah lists him among kings with no share in the world to come (m. Sanhedrin 10:2), but some sages, following Chronicles, held that his repentance was accepted; the Talmud has a tradition that Isaiah was killed under him (b. Yevamot 49b).
The Prayer of Manasseh, a short penitential prayer attributed to him, is included in Orthodox Bibles and in the appendix of the Vulgate, used liturgically as a model of repentance.
Some see the Chronicler's repentance account as theological reinterpretation explaining his long reign; others note Assyrian records of vassal kings summoned to court as making a captivity plausible.

context: He appears as 'Menasi king of Judah' in Assyrian lists of vassals supplying building materials and troops under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. His long reign coincides with the height of Assyrian power.
legacy: His name became shorthand for the apostasy that sealed Judah's fate, and his reported repentance became a classic example of the reach of divine mercy.

traditions.text: Isaiah was put to death by Manasseh, sawn in two while hiding in a tree.
traditions.source: Ascension of Isaiah 5:1-14; Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b

traditions.text: A penitential prayer composed by Manasseh in captivity has been preserved (the Prayer of Manasseh).

voice: Polished, worldly and pragmatic, speaking the language of empire and omens; in the Chronicler's telling, broken and plain-spoken in his repentance.

events.title: Becomes king at eight after Amon's murder
events.summary: The people of the land killed his father's assassins and made the boy Josiah king. He reigned thirty-one years and did not turn aside to the right or the left.

events.title: Begins to seek God and purge idolatry
events.summary: Chronicles places his seeking of God in his eighth year and the beginning of his purge of Judah and Jerusalem in his twelfth year, extending into the former northern territory.

events.title: The book of the law is found
events.summary: During temple repairs in his eighteenth year, Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law. When Shaphan read it to the king, Josiah tore his clothes.

events.title: Consults the prophetess Huldah
events.summary: Huldah confirmed that judgment would come on Jerusalem but promised Josiah that because his heart was tender he would be gathered to his grave in peace before it came.

events.title: Leads a covenant renewal
events.summary: He read the book of the covenant to all the people at the temple and stood by the pillar pledging to keep its commands; the people joined the covenant.

events.title: Sweeping reform of worship
events.summary: He removed vessels for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven, deposed idolatrous priests, defiled Topheth, and destroyed high places from Geba to Beersheba, including those Solomon had built.

events.title: Destroys the altar at Bethel
events.summary: He tore down Jeroboam's altar at Bethel and burned bones on it, fulfilling the word of the man of God from Judah spoken some three centuries earlier, and extended the reform into Samaria's towns.

events.title: Keeps a great Passover
events.summary: He celebrated a Passover according to the book of the covenant; none like it had been kept since the days of the judges.

events.title: Killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho
events.summary: He went out to confront Necho, who was marching to the Euphrates; he was shot by archers (Chronicles) or killed at Megiddo (Kings), and was brought dead to Jerusalem.

events.title: Mourned by Jeremiah and all Judah
events.summary: Jeremiah composed a lament for him, and the mourning became a lasting custom; Zechariah later recalls 'the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon'.

journey.note: Reform begins with the temple and the covenant renewal.
Destroys the northern royal sanctuary.
Removes high places in the cities of Samaria.
Goes out to meet Necho and is killed.
Brought back dead in his chariot and buried.

summary:
Josiah came to the throne of Judah as an eight-year-old after his father Amon was assassinated, and became the most thorough reformer in the history of the monarchy. In his eighteenth year (622 BC), workers repairing the temple found 'the book of the law'. Its reading shook the king; he consulted the prophetess Huldah, gathered the people for a covenant renewal, and launched a purge of foreign cults and local shrines that reached as far as Bethel and the towns of the former northern kingdom, followed by a Passover unmatched since the judges.

Kings gives him its highest praise: no king before or after turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul and might as he did (2 Kgs 23:25). Yet the same narrative states that the reform did not reverse the judgment provoked by Manasseh. In 609 BC Josiah went out to Megiddo against Pharaoh Necho and was killed, aged thirty-nine. Within twenty-three years Jerusalem fell.

Josiah stands at the centre of modern discussion of Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomistic History, since many scholars identify the rediscovered book with some form of Deuteronomy. His reign also forms the background to the early ministries of Jeremiah and Zephaniah.
textSays: 2 Kgs 22:1-23:30 and 2 Chr 34:1-35:27 narrate his reign. Kings centres the reform on the finding of the book (2 Kgs 22:8); Chronicles places the start of the purge six years earlier (2 Chr 34:3). The text predicts his name centuries ahead (1 Kgs 13:2), states that he was unmatched in his turning to the LORD (2 Kgs 23:25), and that the LORD's anger against Judah nevertheless remained (2 Kgs 23:26-27). Chronicles says Necho warned him that God had sent Necho and that Josiah did not listen to words from God's mouth (2 Chr 35:21-22). Jeremiah praises his justice for the poor and needy (Jer 22:15-16).

interpretations.view: Remembered as a righteous king; the Talmud (b. Taanit 22b) explains his death as a failure to consult Jeremiah before engaging Necho, and tradition holds he hid the ark to protect it from exile (b. Yoma 52b).
Read as an example of revival through rediscovery of the word of God, and of personal faithfulness amid national decline; he appears in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:10-11).

Often cited as a model of reformation by Scripture: the book is read, the heart is cut, the covenant is renewed and worship is purified. Some preachers also stress his death as a warning against acting without seeking God's guidance.

Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805) many identify the book with Deuteronomy or an early core of it, and many argue the first edition of Kings was produced to support Josiah's centralisation. Others think the 'finding' account is a later legitimising narrative, and a minority doubt the reform's scope; the debate is ongoing.

strengths: Sought God from his youth
Responded to Scripture with repentance and action
Removed idolatry comprehensively
Defended the cause of the poor and needy
failures: Engaged Necho in battle against warning and was killed (2 Chr 35:22)
turningPoints: Hearing the book of the law read

context: Assyria was collapsing in Josiah's reign (Nineveh fell in 612 BC), opening a window for Judah to reassert control over former northern territory. Necho II was marching to aid the Assyrian remnant against Babylon at Harran and Carchemish when Josiah met him; the Babylonian Chronicle helps date these events.
legacy: Josiah became the ideal king in Deuteronomistic perspective and a fixed point for dating prophets (Jer 1:2; Zeph 1:1). His death was so grieved that lamentation for him became an annual custom (2 Chr 35:25), and his reforms shaped the Torah-centred faith that survived the exile.

traditions.text: Josiah hid the ark of the covenant before the exile, anticipating the destruction of the temple.

voice: Earnest, decisive and devout, young in manner but serious, quick to act once convinced by Scripture; speaks of the book, the covenant and the poor.

events.title: Interprets the book of the law for Josiah
events.summary: Consulted by Josiah's officials, she authenticated the book's warnings as the word of the LORD against Jerusalem and promised Josiah peace in his lifetime because he had humbled himself.

summary: Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem, wife of Shallum the keeper of the wardrobe, living in the Second Quarter. When the book of the law was found in 622 BC, Josiah's officials went to her, not to Jeremiah or Zephaniah, and her oracle confirmed both judgment on Judah and mercy to the king.
textSays: 2 Kgs 22:14-20 and 2 Chr 34:22-28 name her, her husband and her residence, and record her oracle in full.
context: Her consultation is the first recorded instance of a written text being authenticated by a prophet, often noted as an early step toward the idea of Scripture.
legacy: The southern gates of the Second Temple's Temple Mount were called the Huldah Gates (m. Middot 1:3), though the connection to her is uncertain.

traditions.text: Huldah was a relative of Jeremiah and prophesied among the women while he prophesied among the men.

voice: Direct and authoritative, prefacing her words with 'Thus says the LORD' and addressing the king simply as 'the man who sent you'.

events.title: Installed by Nebuchadnezzar
events.summary: After Jehoiachin's deportation Nebuchadnezzar made his uncle Mattaniah king, renaming him Zedekiah and binding him by an oath in God's name.

events.title: Consults Jeremiah secretly but will not obey
events.summary: He repeatedly asked Jeremiah for a word from the LORD and protected him from death, but feared his officials and the Judeans who had defected, and did not surrender as Jeremiah urged.

events.title: Breaks the covenant of slave release
events.summary: During the siege he led a covenant to free Hebrew slaves; when the Babylonians briefly withdrew, owners took them back, and Jeremiah announced judgment.

events.title: Flees, is captured and blinded
events.summary: When the wall was breached he fled by night but was overtaken in the plains of Jericho. At Riblah his sons were killed before his eyes, then he was blinded and taken in chains to Babylon, where he died in prison.

summary: Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, was the last king of Judah, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC. Torn between his officials' pro-Egyptian rebellion and Jeremiah's call to submit to Babylon, he wavered, broke his oath to Nebuchadnezzar, and saw Jerusalem besieged and destroyed. His capture, blinding and exile mark the end of the Davidic monarchy in the land.
textSays: He did evil in the sight of the LORD (2 Kgs 24:19) and did not humble himself before Jeremiah (2 Chr 36:12). Ezekiel condemns his breaking of the oath (Ezek 17:11-21) and foretells that he would be brought to Babylon yet not see it (Ezek 12:12-13), fulfilled when he was blinded before arrival.

interpretations.view: Rabbinic sources sometimes treat him more gently as personally righteous but weak before a wicked generation.
A study in indecision: one who sought the word of God privately but lacked the courage to obey it publicly.

context: Lachish ostraca from the final siege years and the Babylonian Chronicle's record of the 597 capture provide the setting. Debate over 587 versus 586 for Jerusalem's fall depends on how regnal years are reckoned.
legacy: His fate is the closing scene of Kings before the coda on Jehoiachin, and the fall of the city in his eleventh year is lamented in Lamentations and remembered in the fast of the ninth of Av.
voice: Anxious and hesitant, speaking in whispers and asking for secrecy, always weighing what his officials will think.

alternatives.label: Martyred under Manasseh, date unknown (Ascension of Isaiah)

skills.name: Hebrew poetry and rhetoric of the highest order

events.title: Vision of the LORD on the throne and commission
events.summary: In the year Uzziah died he saw the LORD high and lifted up, heard the seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy', confessed his unclean lips, was cleansed with a coal, and volunteered: 'Here am I; send me.' He was sent to a people who would not understand.

events.title: Confronts Ahaz with the Immanuel sign
events.summary: During the Syro-Ephraimite crisis he met Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool with his son Shear-jashub, urged him to trust God rather than Assyria, and gave the sign of a young woman (or virgin) bearing a son called Immanuel.

events.title: Names a son Maher-shalal-hash-baz
events.summary: He wrote the name ('swift to the spoil, quick to the plunder') on a tablet before witnesses and fathered a son by 'the prophetess'; Damascus and Samaria would fall before the child could speak. He and his children were signs in Israel.

events.title: Walks barefoot and stripped for three years
events.summary: When Assyria took Ashdod he went about stripped and barefoot as a sign that Egypt and Cush, Judah's hoped-for allies, would be led captive.

events.title: Warns against alliance with Egypt
events.summary: He condemned envoys going down to Egypt for help, insisting that Egyptians are men and not God.

events.title: Promises deliverance from Sennacherib
events.summary: When Hezekiah sent to him in sackcloth, he answered that the Assyrian king would hear a rumour and return home, and that he would not shoot an arrow into Jerusalem.

events.title: Announces Hezekiah's death, then his healing
events.summary: He told the king to set his house in order; after Hezekiah's prayer he returned with fifteen added years, the sign of the shadow, and a poultice of figs.

events.title: Foretells the Babylonian exile
events.summary: After Hezekiah showed his treasures to Babylonian envoys, he announced that everything would be carried to Babylon and some of the king's descendants would serve in its palace.

events.title: Oracles of comfort and of the Servant
events.summary: The book's later chapters announce comfort to exiled Jerusalem, a return through the wilderness, Cyrus as the LORD's anointed, and a Servant who suffers for the sins of many.

events.title: Vision of new heavens and new earth
events.summary: The book closes with a vision of a renewed creation and all flesh coming to worship.

summary:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem for about forty years in the second half of the eighth century BC, through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. He moved in royal circles, counselled kings face to face, and was married to a woman he calls 'the prophetess'; he gave his sons symbolic names. His call vision in the temple, with its threefold 'Holy', shaped his whole message: the Holy One of Israel demands trust rather than political alliances, judges pride and injustice, and will preserve a remnant.

The book bearing his name is the longest and most quoted prophetic book in the New Testament. Its first part addresses the Assyrian crises of Ahaz and Hezekiah; chapters 36-39 narrate the deliverance of Jerusalem in 701 BC; chapters 40-66 speak to exiles in Babylon and to the restored community, naming Cyrus and presenting the Servant of the LORD. Whether all of this comes from Isaiah himself is one of the classic debates of biblical scholarship.

Isaiah's language of a virgin or young woman bearing Immanuel, a child called Mighty God, a shoot from Jesse's stump, and a Servant 'wounded for our transgressions' became central to Christian proclamation of Jesus, while in Judaism the book is above all the great prophet of consolation read in the synagogue after the ninth of Av.
textSays: The superscription names him son of Amoz and dates his visions to Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isa 1:1). He records his own call (Isa 6:1-13), his encounters with Ahaz (Isa 7:1-25) and Hezekiah (Isa 37:1-39:8; 2 Kgs 19:1-20:19), his wife the prophetess and two sons (Isa 7:3; Isa 8:3), and a three-year sign-act (Isa 20:2-3). Chronicles says he wrote the acts of Uzziah and of Hezekiah (2 Chr 26:22; 2 Chr 32:32). The New Testament quotes passages from across the book as spoken by 'Isaiah' (Matt 3:3; Matt 8:17; John 12:38-41; Acts 8:28-35; Rom 10:16-21).

interpretations.view: Isaiah is the prophet of comfort; the seven haftarot of consolation after the ninth of Av come from Isa 40-66. The Servant of Isa 52:13-53:12 is commonly read as Israel (or the righteous remnant) suffering among the nations, as in Rashi; some ancient sources (e.g. the Targum) apply parts of the passage to the Messiah. Isa 7:14 is read as a young woman of Ahaz's day.

Called 'the fifth evangelist' by Jerome for his clarity about Christ; Isa 7:14 is read with Matt 1:23 as foretelling the virgin birth, and the Sanctus of the liturgy echoes Isa 6:3. The book is read heavily in Advent and Holy Week. Most Catholic scholars now accept multiple authorship as compatible with inspiration.

Many hold to single authorship, citing New Testament attribution (John 12:38-41), predictive prophecy, and the book's unified vocabulary such as 'the Holy One of Israel'. Isa 53 is read as a direct prophecy of Christ's substitutionary death. Others in the same traditions accept a multi-stage book while affirming its messianic witness.

Since Döderlein and Eichhorn in the late 18th century and Duhm (1892), most scholars distinguish First Isaiah (1-39, largely 8th century), Second Isaiah (40-55, an anonymous exilic prophet c. 540s) and Third Isaiah (56-66, early post-exilic), noting the change of historical setting and the naming of Cyrus. Recent work stresses the book's deliberate editorial unity and an Isaianic 'school' carrying his message forward.

strengths: Overwhelmed by God's holiness and willing to go
Courage before kings
Unrivalled poetic vision
Steady counsel of trust in crisis
failures: Confesses himself a man of unclean lips (Isa 6:5)

context: Isaiah's ministry spans the rise of Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III, the fall of Samaria (722 BC), the Ashdod revolt (711 BC) and Sennacherib's invasion (701 BC). The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa, c. 125 BC) is the oldest complete biblical book manuscript, presenting chapters 1-66 as one continuous text.
legacy: Isaiah supplied the New Testament with much of its vocabulary for Christ and the gospel: the voice in the wilderness (Mark 1:3), good news to the poor (Luke 4:17-21), the suffering Servant (Acts 8:32-35), and new heavens and new earth (Rev 21:1). Handel's *Messiah* draws heavily on it. Hebrews' reference to martyrs 'sawn asunder' (Heb 11:37) is widely taken as an allusion to his traditional death.

traditions.text: Isaiah was martyred under Manasseh by being sawn in two with a wooden saw.
traditions.source: Ascension of Isaiah 5:1-14 (Jewish-Christian pseudepigraphon, 1st-2nd c. AD); Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 120

traditions.text: Isaiah hid inside a cedar tree that miraculously opened for him, and Manasseh had the tree sawn through.
traditions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b; Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 10:2

traditions.text: Isaiah was of royal blood, his father Amoz being a brother of King Amaziah.

voice: Majestic and urgent, moving from thunderous indictment to tender comfort; fond of vivid images, wordplay and the phrase 'the Holy One of Israel', and fearless in speaking to kings.

alternatives.label: Holladay: 627 BC is his birth year, not his call
Unknown; last dated in Egypt after 586 BC (Jer 44)
Ministry begins c. 609 if 627 is birth year

events.title: Called as a youth
events.summary: In Josiah's thirteenth year the LORD told him he had been appointed a prophet to the nations before birth. He protested that he was only a youth; the LORD touched his mouth and showed him an almond branch and a boiling pot from the north.

events.title: Forbidden to marry
events.summary: He was told not to take a wife or have children, nor to join funerals or feasts, as a sign of the coming devastation.

events.title: Temple sermon and trial for his life
events.summary: At the start of Jehoiakim's reign he stood in the temple gate and warned that the temple would become like Shiloh. Priests and prophets demanded his death; elders cited Micah's precedent and Ahikam protected him.

events.title: Smashes a potter's flask and is put in the stocks
events.summary: He broke an earthenware flask in the Hinnom valley as a sign of Jerusalem's breaking; Pashhur the priest beat him and put him in the stocks overnight.

events.title: Dictates the scroll that Jehoiakim burns
events.summary: Barred from the temple, he dictated his oracles to Baruch, who read them publicly. The king cut the scroll column by column and burned it; Jeremiah dictated it again with additions.

events.title: Wears a yoke and confronts Hananiah
events.summary: He wore a wooden yoke urging submission to Babylon. The prophet Hananiah broke it and predicted return within two years; Jeremiah announced an iron yoke and Hananiah's death, which followed that year.

events.title: Writes to the exiles in Babylon
events.summary: He told the deported community to build houses, marry, and seek the welfare of the city, for the exile would last seventy years.

events.title: Buys a field at Anathoth during the siege
events.summary: While confined in the guard court, he redeemed his cousin Hanamel's field with sealed deeds as a sign that houses and fields would again be bought in the land.

events.title: Announces the new covenant
events.summary: He foretold a new covenant written on the heart, in which all would know the LORD and sins would be forgiven.

events.title: Thrown into a muddy cistern
events.summary: Officials accused him of weakening the soldiers and lowered him into a cistern where he sank in mud; Ebed-melech the Cushite rescued him with ropes and rags.

events.title: Released by the Babylonians
events.summary: After the city fell, Nebuzaradan freed him at Ramah and let him choose; he stayed in the land with Gedaliah at Mizpah.

events.title: Taken to Egypt against his will
events.summary: After Gedaliah's murder the survivors asked his guidance, then rejected his word to stay and took him and Baruch to Tahpanhes, where he continued to prophesy against Egypt and against the worship of the queen of heaven.

journey.note: Priestly hometown north-east of Jerusalem; his kinsmen there later plotted against him (Jer 11:21-23).
Centre of his ministry: temple gates, palace and guard court.
Freed from chains among the deportees.
Stays with Gedaliah the governor.
Taken to Tahpanhes in the eastern Delta; last recorded ministry.

summary:
Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family at Anathoth, was called as a young man in 627 BC and prophesied for some forty years through the last kings of Judah, the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and its aftermath. Forbidden to marry, opposed by his own townsmen, beaten, imprisoned, and nearly killed more than once, he insisted that Judah's only path was repentance and then submission to Babylon, a message that made him look like a traitor.

The book reveals his inner life more than any other prophet's. In passages often called his 'confessions' he argues with God, curses the day of his birth, and yet finds the word like fire shut up in his bones that he cannot hold in. He performs striking sign-acts: a ruined linen belt, a smashed flask, a wooden yoke, a field purchased while the city is falling. With his scribe Baruch he produced written scrolls of his oracles, one of which King Jehoiakim burned.

Alongside judgment he announced hope: a seventy-year limit to exile, return to the land, and a new covenant written on the heart. That promise became foundational for the New Testament's understanding of Jesus' death and the church (Luke 22:20; Heb 8:8-12). His last known words were spoken in Egypt, where he had been taken against his will.
textSays: The superscription names his father Hilkiah, his town Anathoth, and dates his ministry from Josiah's thirteenth year to the exile (Jer 1:1-3). The book records his call (Jer 1:4-10), his personal laments (Jer 11:18-12:6; Jer 15:10-21; Jer 17:14-18; Jer 18:18-23; Jer 20:7-18), his conflicts with kings, priests and prophets (Jer 20:1-6; Jer 26:1-24; Jer 28:1-17; Jer 36:1-32; Jer 37:11-38:13), and his removal to Egypt (Jer 43:1-7). Chronicles says he lamented Josiah and that the exile fulfilled his word of seventy years (2 Chr 35:25; 2 Chr 36:21-22). Daniel studied his seventy-year prophecy (Dan 9:2), and Matthew quotes him (Matt 2:17-18).

interpretations.view: Jeremiah is the prophet of the destruction, and tradition credits him with Lamentations as well as Kings (b. Bava Batra 15a). Rabbinic literature pictures him as a priest-prophet who mourned Jerusalem and accompanied the exiles part of the way; the new covenant of Jer 31 is read as renewed Torah obedience written on Israel's heart.

Seen as a type of Christ, the innocent sufferer led like a lamb to the slaughter (Jer 11:19) who weeps over Jerusalem. 2 Maccabees portrays him as an intercessor in heaven (2 Macc 15:13-16), supporting the communion of saints. Lamentations is sung in the Tenebrae offices of Holy Week.

The new covenant prophecy is central to covenant theology and to debates about the relationship of Israel and the church: covenant theologians see it fulfilled in the church, while dispensationalists stress a future fulfilment for national Israel as well. Jeremiah is widely held up as a model of faithful ministry without visible success.

Since Duhm and Mowinckel scholars commonly distinguish poetic oracles (often attributed to Jeremiah), biographical prose (often linked with Baruch), and Deuteronomistic-style prose sermons. The Greek Septuagint is about one-eighth shorter with a different order, and Hebrew fragments from Qumran (4QJerb) show both textual forms circulated.

strengths: Persevered for decades without visible success
Honest with God in lament
Courage before kings, priests and crowds
Compassion for his people even while announcing judgment
failures: Bitter despair and cursing his birth (Jer 20:14-18)

context: His ministry spans Josiah's reform, the death of Josiah at Megiddo (609 BC), Babylon's victory at Carchemish (605 BC), the deportations of 597 and 586 BC, and the murder of Gedaliah. Clay seal impressions naming figures from the book, such as Gemariah son of Shaphan and Jehucal son of Shelemiah, have been found in Jerusalem, and the Lachish letters illuminate the final siege.
legacy: Jeremiah gave the church the language of the new covenant and gave Judaism its framework for mourning the temple. His honesty in suffering shaped Christian spirituality, and 'jeremiad' became an English word for a prolonged lament.

traditions.text: Jeremiah was stoned to death by his own people at Tahpanhes in Egypt.
traditions.source: Lives of the Prophets 2 (Jeremiah); cf. Tertullian, Scorpiace 8

traditions.text: Before the fall of Jerusalem Jeremiah hid the tent, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave on the mountain where Moses viewed the land.
Jeremiah is the author of Lamentations.
traditions.source: Septuagint preface to Lamentations; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a

voice: Passionate and raw, swinging between fierce oracles and tears; speaks in vivid images of broken cisterns and potters' clay, and openly argues with God.

events.title: Witnesses Jeremiah's land deed
events.summary: Jeremiah entrusted the sealed and open deeds of the Anathoth field to Baruch to store in an earthenware jar.

events.title: Writes and reads the scroll
events.summary: He wrote Jeremiah's oracles at his dictation and read them in the temple in the chamber of Gemariah; officials advised him and Jeremiah to hide.

events.title: Rewrites the burned scroll
events.summary: After Jehoiakim burned the scroll and ordered their arrest, the LORD hid them, and Baruch wrote a second scroll with many words added.

events.title: Receives a personal oracle
events.summary: When he complained of grief added to his sorrow, God told him not to seek great things for himself but promised to give him his life as a prize of war.

events.title: Taken to Egypt with Jeremiah
events.summary: Accused of turning Jeremiah against the survivors, he was taken with him to Tahpanhes.

summary: Baruch son of Neriah was Jeremiah's scribe and companion, the man who wrote down and publicly read the prophet's oracles and preserved his legal documents. His brother Seraiah was a royal quartermaster (Jer 51:59). Many scholars think the biographical narratives of Jeremiah come from him. A short oracle addressed to him (Jer 45) warns him against ambition and promises survival.
textSays: He appears in Jer 32, 36, 43 and 45 as scribe, reader and companion of Jeremiah, and goes with him to Egypt.

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition counts him among the prophets and makes him Ezra's teacher in Babylon, explaining that Ezra did not return to Jerusalem while Baruch lived (b. Megillah 16b).
The book of Baruch, attributed to him, is deuterocanonical and includes the Letter of Jeremiah as its sixth chapter.

The book of Baruch is classed as apocryphal and dated to the Hellenistic period; 2 Baruch and 3 Baruch are later pseudepigrapha. Baruch is valued as a model of the faithful helper behind a public ministry.

context: Two clay bullae reading 'Belonging to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' surfaced on the antiquities market in the 1970s and 1990s; their authenticity has been questioned, and several scholars now treat them as possible forgeries.
legacy: A cluster of later writings under his name (1-4 Baruch) shows how prominent he became as a bridge figure between the prophets and the scribes.

traditions.text: Baruch wrote a book read to the exiles in Babylon, now the deuterocanonical Book of Baruch.

voice: Careful, precise and loyal, with a scribe's attention to wording; occasionally voices his own weariness and disappointed hopes.

aliases: son of man (as God addresses him)

alternatives.label: If 'thirtieth year' (Ezek 1:1) refers to another era, e.g. Josiah's reform, his birth is unknown

skills.name: Priestly knowledge of temple and ritual

gifts.name: Visions of the glory of God

events.title: Deported with King Jehoiachin
events.summary: He was among the leading citizens taken to Babylonia in 597 BC; he dates his oracles by the years of Jehoiachin's exile.

events.title: Vision of the throne-chariot by the Chebar
events.summary: In the fifth year of the exile the heavens opened and he saw four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with the likeness of the glory of the LORD.

events.title: Commissioned and made a watchman
events.summary: He was sent to a rebellious house, given a scroll to eat that tasted like honey, sat stunned among the exiles at Tel-abib for seven days, and was appointed a watchman responsible to warn.

events.title: Enacts the siege of Jerusalem
events.summary: He drew Jerusalem on a brick, lay on his left side 390 days and on his right side 40, ate rationed bread, and shaved his head and beard, dividing the hair to show the fate of the city.

events.title: Carried in vision to the defiled temple
events.summary: Lifted by a lock of his hair, he saw idolatry in the temple courts, then watched the glory of the LORD leave the temple and stand over the mountain east of the city.

events.title: Digs through the wall as an exile
events.summary: He packed an exile's baggage and dug through the wall at dusk with his face covered, a sign of the prince's flight and capture.

events.title: Death of his wife
events.summary: Told that the delight of his eyes would be taken, he did not mourn when his wife died, as a sign that the exiles would be too stunned to mourn the fall of the temple.

events.title: News of Jerusalem's fall; his mouth is opened
events.summary: A fugitive arrived reporting that the city had been struck; the evening before, his mouth had been opened and he was no longer mute.

events.title: Valley of dry bones
events.summary: In a valley full of bones he prophesied, and they came together and lived when breath entered them: a picture of the whole house of Israel restored from the grave of exile.

events.title: Vision of the new temple and the river
events.summary: In the twenty-fifth year of exile he toured a measured, ideal temple, saw the glory return, and saw a river flow from it to heal the Dead Sea. The city's new name would be 'The LORD is there'.

events.title: Last dated oracle
events.summary: In the twenty-seventh year he announced that Egypt would be given to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for the long, unrewarded siege of Tyre.

journey.note: Priestly upbringing in Jerusalem before deportation.
Deported with Jehoiachin to Babylonia.
Settled at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal near Nippur, where he received his call.
Visionary journey to the temple (in the Spirit, not bodily).
Returned in vision to the exiles and told them all he had seen.

summary:
Ezekiel son of Buzi was a priest deported to Babylonia with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. Five years later, beside the Chebar canal, he saw the glory of God enthroned above living creatures and wheels, and was commissioned to speak to a rebellious people whether they listened or not. For more than twenty years he ministered among the exiles at Tel-abib, where the elders came to sit in his house.

His ministry falls into two halves divided by the fall of Jerusalem. Before 586 BC he insisted, against the exiles' hopes, that the city and temple would be destroyed because of idolatry; he acted this out through startling sign-acts and long allegories of Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife, and he saw the glory of God depart from the temple. After the news of the city's fall reached him, his message turned to restoration: a new heart and spirit, a shepherd-king from David's line, dry bones raised, and a renewed temple from which a life-giving river flows.

Ezekiel addresses the individual's responsibility before God (Ezek 18), the honour of God's name among the nations, and the reality of God's presence outside the land. His imagery is reused extensively in the book of Revelation.
textSays: He identifies himself as a priest, son of Buzi, among the exiles by the Chebar, and dates his call to the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile (Ezek 1:1-3). God consistently addresses him as 'son of man' (Ezek 2:1). He was made a watchman (Ezek 3:17; Ezek 33:7), was periodically unable to speak except to deliver God's word (Ezek 3:26-27; Ezek 24:27; Ezek 33:22), lived in a house where elders consulted him (Ezek 8:1; Ezek 14:1; Ezek 20:1), and was widowed (Ezek 24:18). He was regarded by the exiles as an entertaining singer whose words they did not obey (Ezek 33:30-33).

interpretations.view: The opening chariot vision (merkavah) was considered so profound that its public exposition was restricted (m. Hagigah 2:1), and it became the basis of early Jewish mysticism. The temple of chapters 40-48 is generally understood as the future, third temple; differences from the Torah's laws were so troubling that the book's canonicity was questioned until Hananiah ben Hezekiah reconciled them (b. Shabbat 13b).

The closed east gate (Ezek 44:1-3) has been read since the Fathers as a figure of Mary's perpetual virginity, and the river from the temple (Ezek 47) as baptism and the Spirit. The four living creatures became the symbols of the four evangelists.
Chapters 40-48 describe a literal temple to be built in the millennial kingdom, with memorial sacrifices; chapters 38-39 describe a future invasion of Israel by Gog.

The visionary temple is a symbolic portrait of God dwelling with his redeemed people, fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation (John 2:19-21; Rev 21:22-22:2); Gog and Magog are read as a figure of final opposition (Rev 20:8).

strengths: Obedience in costly and humiliating sign-acts
Faithfulness as watchman to an unresponsive audience
Profound vision of God's holiness and presence
failures: Protests at defiling food, showing priestly scruple (Ezek 4:14)
Initially sits in bitterness and heat of spirit (Ezek 3:14-15)
turningPoints: Seeing the glory leave the temple

context: The Judean exiles of 597 BC were settled in agricultural communities in central Babylonia. The Chebar (Akkadian *naru kabari*) is attested in cuneiform tablets from Nippur, and the Al-Yahudu tablets document Judean villages in Babylonia in this period. Tyre's thirteen-year siege by Nebuchadnezzar is reported by Josephus (*Against Apion* 1.21).
legacy: Ezekiel gave Judaism and Christianity a theology of God's presence beyond the temple and land, the promise of a new heart and spirit (Ezek 36:26-27), and the images of the good shepherd (Ezek 34; John 10:11), the river of life (Rev 22:1-2), and the measured holy city (Rev 21:10-17).

traditions.text: Ezekiel was killed in Babylon by a leader of the exiled Israelites whom he had rebuked for idolatry, and was buried in the tomb of Shem and Arphaxad.
Ezekiel's tomb is venerated at al-Kifl, south of Babylon, a pilgrimage site for Jews and later Muslims.

voice: Intense, formal and priestly, given to precise dates and measurements; his speech alternates between stark, almost shocking imagery and lofty visions, and he often repeats 'then you shall know that I am the LORD'.

alternatives.label: Last dated appearance: third year of Cyrus (Dan 10:1)
If Dan 1:1 uses Babylonian accession-year reckoning vs. Jer 25:1 (Judean)

skills.name: Literature and language of the Chaldeans

events.title: Taken to Babylon as a young noble
events.summary: In the third year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and took young men of royal and noble families for training; Daniel was renamed Belteshazzar.

events.title: Refuses the king's food
events.summary: Resolving not to defile himself with the king's food and wine, he proposed a ten-day test of vegetables and water; he and his friends emerged healthier and ten times wiser than the king's magicians.

events.title: Reveals and interprets Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream
events.summary: When the wise men faced execution for failing to tell the king his dream, Daniel and his friends prayed; he revealed a statue of four metals struck by a stone that became a mountain, and was made ruler over the province of Babylon.

events.title: Interprets the dream of the great tree
events.summary: He told Nebuchadnezzar that the felled tree was the king himself, who would be driven from people until he acknowledged that the Most High rules, and urged him to break off his sins by righteousness.

events.title: Vision of four beasts and the son of man
events.summary: In Belshazzar's first year he saw four beasts from the sea and one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days to receive an everlasting kingdom.

events.title: Vision of the ram and the goat at Susa
events.summary: In vision he was at Susa by the Ulai canal and saw a ram (Media-Persia) overthrown by a goat (Greece), whose little horn would desecrate the sanctuary. Gabriel explained it, and Daniel was ill for days.

events.title: Reads the writing on the wall
events.summary: At Belshazzar's feast using the temple vessels, a hand wrote on the wall. Daniel read 'Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin' as the end of the kingdom; that night Belshazzar was killed and Darius the Mede received the kingdom.

events.title: Prayer and the seventy weeks
events.summary: Reading Jeremiah's seventy years, he confessed Israel's sin and prayed for Jerusalem; Gabriel announced seventy 'weeks' leading to the coming of an anointed one and the end of sacrifice.

events.title: Delivered from the lions' den
events.summary: Rival officials secured a decree forbidding prayer to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem three times a day as usual, was thrown to the lions, and was found unharmed in the morning.

events.title: Final vision by the Tigris
events.summary: In the third year of Cyrus, after three weeks of mourning, he saw a man clothed in linen and received a detailed revelation of kings of the north and south, a time of trouble, and the resurrection of many to everlasting life or contempt.

journey.note: Youth among Judah's nobility.
Deported and trained for royal service; remained through the fall of Babylon.
Present at Susa in a vision (whether bodily or in the Spirit is debated); Dan 8:27 implies he was on the king's business.

summary:
Daniel was a young man of Judah's nobility deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles. Trained in Babylonian learning and renamed Belteshazzar, he rose to high office under Nebuchadnezzar and continued in public life into the Persian period. The first half of his book (chapters 1-6) tells stories of faithfulness at a foreign court: refusing the king's food, interpreting dreams, reading the writing on the wall, and surviving the lions' den. In each, God vindicates those who refuse to compromise and humbles proud kings.

The second half (chapters 7-12) records Daniel's own visions: four beasts and a son of man given an everlasting kingdom, a ram and goat, seventy 'weeks' of years, and a long revelation of conflicts culminating in resurrection. These apocalyptic chapters shaped Jewish and Christian hope; Jesus called himself the Son of Man and spoke of 'the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet' (Matt 24:15).

The date of the book is among the most debated questions in Old Testament study. Traditional readers take it as written by Daniel in the sixth century BC, with genuine predictive prophecy. Most critical scholars date its final form to about 167-164 BC, during the persecution by Antiochus IV, with the visions functioning as history written as prophecy up to that crisis. Many others hold intermediate views, with older court tales collected and the visions added later.
textSays: Daniel was taken in the third year of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1-6), served the king until Cyrus's first year (Dan 1:21), and received a vision in Cyrus's third year (Dan 10:1). He was set over the wise men of Babylon (Dan 2:48), served Belshazzar as third ruler (Dan 5:29) and Darius as one of three chief officials (Dan 6:2). He prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10). Ezekiel names a Daniel with Noah and Job as a model of righteousness and wisdom (Ezek 14:14; Ezek 14:20; Ezek 28:3). Jesus refers to 'Daniel the prophet' (Matt 24:15), and Hebrews alludes to those who stopped the mouths of lions (Heb 11:33).

interpretations.view: Daniel is placed among the Writings rather than the Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, and the Talmud does not count him a prophet in the same sense (b. Megillah 3a), though he was greater in wisdom. His fidelity to dietary law and prayer became a model for diaspora Jews; the seventy weeks have been read as ending with the destruction of the Second Temple.

Daniel is one of the four major prophets. Their Bibles include the Greek additions: the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men in chapter 3, and the stories of Susanna and Bel and the Dragon. The stone cut without hands (Dan 2:34) was read by the Fathers as Christ born of the Virgin, and the son of man (Dan 7:13) as Christ.

Sixth-century authorship is defended on grounds of Jesus' attribution, fragments of Daniel at Qumran close to the proposed Maccabean date, the accurate portrait of Belshazzar as co-regent, and the possibility of predictive prophecy. The seventy weeks are often calculated to reach Jesus' ministry and death. Dispensationalists separate the seventieth week as a future tribulation; others see it fulfilled in Christ's first coming.

Most date the final book to c. 167-164 BC: chapter 11 tracks Hellenistic history in detail up to Antiochus IV's persecution but is inaccurate about his death, suggesting composition before 164 BC. Problems cited include Darius the Mede, unknown outside Daniel, and Belshazzar called Nebuchadnezzar's son. Defenders reply that 'son' can mean successor and that Darius may be a title for Gubaru or for Cyrus himself (reading Dan 6:28 as 'Darius, that is, Cyrus').

strengths: Uncompromising faithfulness in small and great matters
Wisdom and integrity in government; rivals found no fault (Dan 6:4)
Habitual prayer and confession
Humility in interpreting dreams (Dan 2:30)
failures: None recorded; he confesses the nation's sins as his own (Dan 9:20)
turningPoints: Deportation and the decision about the king's food

context: The Nabonidus Cylinder and the Verse Account of Nabonidus confirm that Belshazzar was Nabonidus' son who ruled Babylon while his father stayed at Tayma, explaining why Daniel could only be made 'third' ruler. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's campaign in the west in 605 BC. Eight manuscripts of Daniel were found at Qumran, the earliest (4QDanc) dated to the late second century BC.
legacy: Daniel provided the template for apocalyptic literature and the language of the Son of Man, the resurrection of the dead (Dan 12:2), and the succession of world empires. Revelation draws on his beasts and visions. His stories have long encouraged believers living as minorities under hostile powers.

traditions.text: Daniel died in Babylon and was buried in the royal tomb with honour.
Daniel's tomb is at Susa (Shush, Iran), where a shrine has been venerated since at least the medieval period.
traditions.source: Benjamin of Tudela, *Itinerary* (12th c.); local tradition

traditions.text: Daniel exposed the fraud of the priests of Bel and killed the dragon, and was again thrown to lions, being fed by the prophet Habakkuk.
traditions.source: Bel and the Dragon 1-42 (Greek additions to Daniel)

voice: Calm, courteous and measured, deferential to kings without flattering them; speaks with the polish of a court scholar but turns quickly to confession and prayer, always giving credit to the God of heaven.
