events.title: Trained in Babylon and renamed
events.summary: Hananiah was renamed Shadrach and, with Daniel, Mishael and Azariah, kept from the king's food and excelled in wisdom.

events.title: Thrown into the fiery furnace
events.summary: With Meshach and Abednego he refused to worship the golden image; they told the king God could deliver them, 'but if not' they still would not bow. They walked unharmed in the furnace with a fourth figure and were promoted.

summary: Shadrach (Hananiah) was one of Daniel's three Judean companions in Babylon. Appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, he is remembered for refusing to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and surviving the fiery furnace.
textSays: He appears in Dan 1:6-20, Dan 2:17-18 (praying with Daniel), Dan 2:49 (appointed), and Dan 3:1-30.
legacy: The three are cited as examples of faith that 'quenched the violence of fire' (Heb 11:34) and are commemorated in Orthodox and Catholic calendars on 17 December; the Greek additions give them a prayer and a hymn (the Benedicite).

traditions.text: The three young men sang the hymn of praise later called the Benedicite while walking in the furnace.
traditions.source: Song of the Three Young Men (Greek additions to Daniel 3)

voice: Plain and resolute, speaking with his companions as one voice: respectful to the king but unbending.

names.meaning: Hebrew name Mishael: who is what God is?; Babylonian name of uncertain meaning

roles: Administrator of the province of Babylon

events.title: Trained in Babylon and renamed
events.summary: Mishael was renamed Meshach and with his companions excelled the king's wise men.

events.title: Survives the fiery furnace
events.summary: He refused to worship the golden image and was thrown bound into the furnace, emerging without even the smell of fire.

summary: Meshach (Mishael) was one of Daniel's three companions, appointed over the province of Babylon, who refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar's image and was delivered from the fiery furnace.
textSays: He appears in Dan 1:6-20, Dan 2:17-18, Dan 2:49 and Dan 3:1-30.
legacy: Remembered with his companions in Heb 11:34 and in the Greek additions to Daniel; 1 Maccabees lists the three as examples of faith (1 Macc 2:59).
voice: Quiet and steady, speaking with his companions as one voice of resolute trust.

names.meaning: Hebrew name Azariah: the LORD has helped; Babylonian name possibly 'servant of Nabu'

roles: Administrator of the province of Babylon

events.title: Trained in Babylon and renamed
events.summary: Azariah was renamed Abednego, a name that may honour the Babylonian god Nabu, and with his companions excelled in wisdom.

events.title: Survives the fiery furnace
events.summary: He refused to bow to the golden image; the king saw four men walking loose in the fire and called them out, praising their God.

summary: Abednego (Azariah) was one of Daniel's three companions in Babylon who refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and was delivered from the fiery furnace, after which the king forbade any word against their God.
textSays: He appears in Dan 1:6-20, Dan 2:17-18, Dan 2:49 and Dan 3:1-30.
legacy: The Greek additions to Daniel attribute to him (as Azariah) a long prayer of confession in the furnace, the Prayer of Azariah.

traditions.text: Azariah prayed a prayer of national confession while standing in the furnace.
traditions.source: Prayer of Azariah (Greek additions to Daniel 3)

voice: Earnest and devout, inclined to prayer and confession, speaking with his companions as one voice.

names.meaning: O Nabu, protect my heir (or boundary)

events.title: Defeats Egypt at Carchemish
events.summary: As crown prince he routed Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish, after which Egypt no longer came out of its land.

events.title: First deportation from Jerusalem
events.summary: He besieged Jerusalem, took King Jehoiachin, the temple treasures and the leading citizens to Babylon, and installed Zedekiah.

events.title: Destroys Jerusalem and the temple
events.summary: After an eighteen-month siege his forces broke through; the temple, palace and houses were burned and the walls torn down.

events.title: Dreams of the statue and the tree; sets up the golden image
events.summary: Daniel portrays him as troubled by dreams, raging and then acknowledging Daniel's God, erecting a golden image, and finally humbled by seven periods of madness before praising the Most High.

summary: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 605 to 562 BC, the most powerful king of his age. He crushed Egypt at Carchemish, deported Judah's elite in 597 BC, and destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple in 586 BC. Jeremiah calls him the LORD's servant, an instrument of judgment (Jer 25:9; Jer 27:6), while Daniel depicts a proud king brought to confess that the Most High rules the kingdom of men.
textSays: Kings, Chronicles and Jeremiah narrate his campaigns against Judah (2 Kgs 24:1-25:21; 2 Chr 36:6-20; Jer 39:1-10). Ezekiel speaks of his siege of Tyre and campaign against Egypt (Ezek 26:7-14; Ezek 29:17-20). Daniel narrates his dreams, his image and his madness and restoration (Dan 1:1-4:37).

interpretations.view: His humbling in Daniel 4 is read as a historical event and an example of God's sovereignty over pagan rulers; some Christian readers have hoped he genuinely came to faith.

Many suggest the madness story preserves memories of Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king, who withdrew to Tayma for ten years; a Qumran text, the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), tells a similar story of Nabonidus afflicted for seven years. Others note that Babylonian sources for Nebuchadnezzar's later reign are sparse.

context: The Babylonian Chronicles record his capture of 'the city of Judah' on 2 Adar of his seventh year (16 March 597 BC). He rebuilt Babylon with the Ishtar Gate and processional way; tens of thousands of bricks bear his name. Ration tablets from Babylon list 'Ya'u-kinu king of Judah' (Jehoiachin).
legacy: He became the archetype of the proud world ruler, and 'Babylon' a symbol of godless empire (Rev 17:5; Rev 18:2).
voice: Imperious and expansive, boasting of the great Babylon he built; volatile, swinging from fury to extravagant praise of whatever god has impressed him.

events.title: Called by name as God's shepherd and anointed
events.summary: Isaiah names him as the LORD's shepherd who will say of Jerusalem 'she shall be built', and his anointed whom God grasps by the right hand, though Cyrus does not know him.

events.title: Conquers Babylon
events.summary: Persian forces took Babylon in October 539 BC; Daniel records Belshazzar's death that night and Daniel's continued service under Cyrus.

events.title: Decree permitting the return and temple rebuilding
events.summary: In his first year he proclaimed that the God of heaven had charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and allowed any of his people to go up.

events.title: Returns the temple vessels
events.summary: He had his treasurer count out the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken and hand them to Sheshbazzar.

summary: Cyrus II, founder of the Persian Empire, conquered Media, Lydia and in 539 BC Babylon. His policy of allowing deported peoples to return and restore their sanctuaries enabled the first return of Jewish exiles in 538 BC. Remarkably, Isaiah names him as the LORD's shepherd and anointed, the only foreign ruler given that title in the Bible.
textSays: Scripture presents his decree as the fulfilment of Jeremiah's word, issued because the LORD stirred his spirit (Ezra 1:1; 2 Chr 36:22). Isaiah names him in advance (Isa 44:28; Isa 45:1-13). Daniel served into his reign (Dan 1:21; Dan 6:28; Dan 10:1).

interpretations.view: Honoured as a righteous gentile instrument of redemption; the Talmud debates whether he was truly righteous since he later halted the building (b. Rosh Hashanah 4a).
The naming of Cyrus some 150 years in advance is cited as predictive prophecy, and Cyrus as a type of Christ the deliverer who frees captives.
The naming of Cyrus is a principal reason for dating Isa 40-55 to the 540s BC, when an exilic prophet saw his rise as the LORD's doing.

context: The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BC), found in Babylon in 1879, records his restoration of gods and peoples to their homes, consistent with Ezra's decree though it does not mention Judah. Herodotus (*Histories* 1.214) reports his death in battle against the Massagetae in 530 BC; he was buried at Pasargadae.
legacy: Cyrus became a model of the tolerant gentile ruler used by God, invoked in later Jewish and modern political rhetoric about restoration to Zion.

traditions.text: Cyrus read Isaiah's prophecy about himself and was moved to fulfil it.

voice: Magnanimous and politically astute, speaking in the grand style of royal proclamation, generous to subject peoples and their gods.

names.meaning: Esther possibly from Persian 'star' or Babylonian Ishtar; Hadassah means 'myrtle'

alternatives.label: Book read as historical novella; no fixed date

skills.name: Legal authority to establish a festival

events.title: Vashti deposed
events.summary: In his third year King Ahasuerus held a vast feast; when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his command, she was removed and a search for a new queen begun.

events.title: Taken into the palace and made queen
events.summary: Esther, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, was gathered with other young women; she won Hegai's and then the king's favour and was crowned in the seventh year.

events.title: Conceals her people
events.summary: On Mordecai's instruction she did not reveal her people or kindred.

events.title: Reports a plot against the king
events.summary: Mordecai discovered a plot by two eunuchs and told Esther, who informed the king in Mordecai's name; it was recorded in the chronicles.

events.title: Haman's decree of annihilation
events.summary: Angered that Mordecai would not bow, Haman obtained a decree to destroy all Jews on a date chosen by lot (pur).

events.title: 'For such a time as this'
events.summary: Mordecai urged her to plead with the king, warning that relief would arise from another place if she kept silent and asking whether she had come to the kingdom for such a time. She called a three-day fast: 'if I perish, I perish.'

events.title: Approaches the king unsummoned
events.summary: Risking death, she stood in the inner court; the king held out the golden sceptre. She invited him and Haman to a banquet, then to a second.

events.title: Exposes Haman
events.summary: At the second banquet she revealed that she and her people had been sold to destruction and named Haman as the enemy. Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.

events.title: Secures a counter-decree
events.summary: Falling at the king's feet in tears, she pleaded for the decree to be reversed; a new edict allowed the Jews to defend themselves.

events.title: Establishes Purim
events.summary: After the Jews' victory, Mordecai and then Queen Esther with full authority wrote to confirm the annual days of Purim.

summary:
Esther (Hadassah) was a Jewish orphan of the tribe of Benjamin, raised in Susa by her cousin Mordecai, who became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes I (486-465 BC). When the royal official Haman secured an empire-wide decree to annihilate the Jews, Mordecai urged her to intervene. After a three-day fast she approached the king uninvited at the risk of her life, outmanoeuvred Haman through two banquets, and obtained a counter-decree that allowed her people to defend themselves.

The book named for her is famous for never mentioning God by name, though fasting, providential 'coincidences' (a sleepless king, a reversal of fortunes) and Mordecai's hint that deliverance would arise 'from another place' point to hidden divine action. It explains the origin of Purim, the festival of lots, and Esther herself issues a written decree confirming it.

Esther has been read as a model of courage, of faithful presence within a foreign power, and of a woman's decisive leadership. Questions about the book's historicity and about its Greek form, which adds explicit prayers and mentions of God, have made it one of the most discussed books of the canon.
textSays: She is daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, and was adopted by Mordecai (Esth 2:7; Esth 2:15). She was made queen in the seventh year of Ahasuerus (Esth 2:16-17), concealed her identity (Esth 2:10), risked death to approach the king (Esth 4:11-16), exposed Haman (Esth 7:3-6), and wrote with full authority to confirm Purim (Esth 9:29-32). The Hebrew text never names God.

interpretations.view: The Megillah is read publicly at Purim with noisemakers drowning Haman's name. Rabbinic tradition sees God's hiddenness (hester panim) wordplayed in her name and counts her among seven prophetesses (b. Megillah 14a). Some sages discussed whether she was blameless in marrying a gentile king, concluding she acted under compulsion.

Their canon includes the Greek additions (some 107 verses): Mordecai's dream, the text of the royal decrees, and prayers of Mordecai and Esther that make God's role explicit. Esther interceding before the king is read as a figure of Mary interceding for the faithful.

The Hebrew book alone is canonical. It is valued as a study in providence, where God works through ordinary events without miracle. Luther voiced strong reservations about the book; most Protestant traditions have nonetheless embraced it as Scripture.

Many scholars read Esther as a historical novella or diaspora court tale, citing Herodotus' statement that Xerxes' queen was Amestris, the improbable scale of the events, and the absence of Esther in Persian records. Others defend a historical core, noting accurate details of Persian court life and the attestation of an official named Marduka at Susa in the Persepolis tablets.

strengths: Teachable and obedient to Mordecai
Courage to risk her life
Strategic patience and timing
Leadership in fasting and in law-giving
turningPoints: Mordecai's challenge 'for such a time as this'

context: Susa (Shushan) was one of the Persian royal capitals; French excavations uncovered the palace of Darius and Xerxes with its audience hall. Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and its canonicity was still discussed by some rabbis in the early centuries AD.
legacy: Purim remains one of the most joyful Jewish festivals. Esther's words 'if I perish, I perish' and Mordecai's 'for such a time as this' are among the most quoted lines in Scripture for courageous action.

traditions.text: Esther and Mordecai are buried in Hamadan (ancient Ecbatana), Iran, where a tomb shrine is venerated by Iranian Jews.
traditions.source: Local Jewish tradition; noted by medieval travellers

traditions.text: Esther prayed a long prayer in sackcloth and ashes before approaching the king.

voice: Poised and gracious, choosing words carefully and never rushing; beneath the courtly manner, resolute: 'if I perish, I perish.'

names.meaning: Likely derived from the Babylonian god Marduk

events.title: Raises his orphaned cousin Esther
events.summary: A Benjaminite descended from Kish, he adopted Hadassah when her parents died.

events.title: Uncovers a plot against the king
events.summary: Sitting in the king's gate, he learned of a conspiracy by Bigthan and Teresh and reported it through Esther.

events.title: Refuses to bow to Haman
events.summary: He would not bow or pay homage to Haman, telling the officials he was a Jew; Haman resolved to destroy all Jews.

events.title: Mourns and challenges Esther
events.summary: He put on sackcloth and urged Esther to plead for her people, suggesting she had come to the kingdom for such a time.

events.title: Honoured and promoted
events.summary: The sleepless king read of his loyalty and had Haman parade him through the city; he later received the king's signet ring and became second to the king, seeking the welfare of his people.

summary: Mordecai was a Benjaminite official in Susa who raised his cousin Esther. His refusal to bow to Haman triggered the threat against the Jews, and his challenge moved Esther to act. After Haman's fall he was given the king's signet ring, rose to be second only to the king, and with Esther established the feast of Purim.
textSays: His genealogy runs through Jair, Shimei and Kish of Benjamin, and he or his ancestor was carried away with Jehoiachin (Esth 2:5-6; the antecedent of 'who' is debated, since Mordecai himself would be very old). The book ends praising his greatness (Esth 10:3).

interpretations.view: Honoured as a sage and as one of the returnees named in Ezra 2:2; his refusal to bow is explained as refusal to give honour bordering on worship, or as the ancient enmity between Saul's line (Kish) and Agag's (Haman the Agagite).
Read as a model of principled loyalty to God and of providence working through ordinary faithfulness.

context: A Persepolis Fortification Tablet names an official Marduka at Susa in the time of Darius I or Xerxes; some identify him with Mordecai, though the name was common.
legacy: Purim was once called 'Mordecai's day' (2 Macc 15:36).
voice: Grave, principled and politically shrewd, speaking in short decisive sentences; carries the authority of an elder guardian.

skills.name: Expert in the Law of Moses
Teaching and public reading of Scripture

events.title: Commissioned by Artaxerxes
events.summary: The king's letter authorised him to lead volunteers to Jerusalem, carry silver and gold for the temple, and appoint magistrates who knew the law of his God, with power to teach and enforce it.

events.title: Gathers the returnees at the Ahava canal
events.summary: Finding no Levites among them, he sent for some from Casiphia before departing.

events.title: Fasts rather than request an escort
events.summary: Ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after declaring God's protection, he proclaimed a fast for a safe journey.

events.title: Arrives in Jerusalem
events.summary: After about four months, the company arrived, delivered the weighed treasures, and offered sacrifices.

events.title: Mourns over mixed marriages
events.summary: Told that many, including leaders, had married women of surrounding peoples, he tore his garments, pulled out his hair, and prayed a confession at the evening sacrifice.

events.title: Covenant to put away foreign wives
events.summary: A great assembly gathered in heavy rain; a commission investigated cases over three months, and a list of offenders closes the book.

events.title: Reads the Law at the Water Gate
events.summary: Standing on a wooden platform from dawn to midday, he read the book of the Law while Levites explained it; the people wept and were told to celebrate instead.

events.title: Feast of Booths and covenant renewal
events.summary: The people kept Booths as not since Joshua's day, with daily reading, then confessed their sins in a long prayer of Israel's history.

events.title: Leads a choir at the wall's dedication
events.summary: Ezra the scribe went before one of the processions on the wall.

journey.note: Departs on the first day of the first month.
Arrives on the first day of the fifth month, a journey of about 1,400 km.

summary:
Ezra was a priest descended from Aaron and a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses who led a second wave of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem under the Persian king Artaxerxes. The text sums up his life in one sentence: he had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to do it, and to teach its statutes in Israel (Ezra 7:10). Commissioned by the king to bring offerings for the temple and to establish the Law as the governing code of the Jews in the province, he arrived after a four-month journey made without military escort.

In Jerusalem he confronted widespread intermarriage with surrounding peoples, a practice he saw as repeating the sins that had led to exile; his prayer of confession and the resulting covenant to dissolve such marriages are among the hardest passages in the Old Testament for modern readers. In Nehemiah he reappears reading the Law aloud to the assembled people with Levites explaining it, an event often seen as the birth of synagogue-style Scripture exposition.

Jewish tradition remembers Ezra as a second Moses who restored the Torah to Israel. The relative chronology of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated: the biblical order places Ezra first (458 BC), while some scholars place him after Nehemiah (398 BC).
textSays: His priestly genealogy runs to Aaron (Ezra 7:1-5). He was a scribe skilled in the Law, and the hand of the LORD was on him (Ezra 7:6). He came in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:7-8), bearing a royal letter (Ezra 7:11-26). Ezra 7:27-9:15 is written in the first person. He led reforms on intermarriage (Ezra 9:1-10:44) and read the Law publicly (Neh 8:1-18).

interpretations.view: Ezra is honoured as the restorer of Torah, worthy to have received it had Moses not preceded him (b. Sanhedrin 21b). He is credited with introducing the square Assyrian script, founding the Great Assembly, and instituting Torah readings on Mondays and Thursdays (b. Bava Kamma 82a).
Honoured as a holy priest and scribe. The Esdras literature is numbered differently: 1 Esdras is canonical in Orthodox churches, and 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) appears in the appendix of the Vulgate.

Seen as a model of expository ministry and of reform grounded in Scripture. His marriage reform is defended by some as necessary for preserving covenant faith, and seen by others as a culturally bound measure to be read alongside Ruth and Jonah's openness to outsiders.

Debate centres on chronology (458 vs 398 BC), the authenticity of Artaxerxes' Aramaic letter, and the nature of 'the Law' he brought, which some identify with the completed Pentateuch, making Ezra pivotal in its final shaping.

strengths: Disciplined study, practice and teaching of Scripture
Faith that refused a military escort
Deep identification with his people's sin in prayer
failures: None recorded; his marriage reform is a matter of interpretive debate rather than narrated failure
turningPoints: The public reading of the Law

context: Judah was a small Persian province (Yehud). Persian kings sometimes authorised local law codes, as with the Egyptian legal codification under Darius I. The Elephantine papyri (late 5th century BC) show a Jewish community in Egypt in contact with Jerusalem and Samaria and help date Nehemiah's contemporaries.
legacy: Ezra's model of the scribe-teacher anticipated the rabbis and the Christian teaching office. His public reading with interpretation (Neh 8:8) is widely seen as a forerunner of the sermon. Pseudepigraphal books under his name (1 and 2 Esdras, 4 Ezra) shaped later apocalyptic thought.

traditions.text: Ezra wrote his own book and the genealogies of Chronicles.
Ezra, inspired, dictated the twenty-four books of Scripture and seventy hidden books after they had been burned.
Ezra died in old age and was buried with great honour in Jerusalem.
A tomb of Ezra is venerated at al-Uzair on the Tigris in southern Iraq.
traditions.source: Local tradition; noted by Benjamin of Tudela, *Itinerary*

voice: Learned and devout, measured in speech until moved to grief; quotes the Law readily and prays in long, penitent sentences that include himself among the guilty.

events.title: Hears of Jerusalem's broken walls
events.summary: In the month Kislev of Artaxerxes' twentieth year, his brother Hanani reported that the survivors were in disgrace and the walls broken. He wept, fasted and prayed, confessing Israel's sins and appealing to God's promise.

events.title: Requests leave from the king
events.summary: Serving wine, he was asked why he was sad; after a silent prayer he requested to be sent to rebuild the city, along with letters for safe passage and timber.

events.title: Night inspection of the walls
events.summary: Three days after arriving, he rode around the ruined walls by night, then called the leaders to rise and build.

events.title: Organises the rebuilding by families
events.summary: Priests, goldsmiths, perfumers, district rulers and daughters each repaired assigned sections, often in front of their own houses.

events.title: Builds with sword and trowel
events.summary: Against mockery and threatened attack by Sanballat, Tobiah, Arabs and Ashdodites, he armed the builders, set guards, and kept a trumpeter beside him.

events.title: Ends exploitation of the poor
events.summary: Hearing that the poor were mortgaging fields and selling children to wealthier Jews, he rebuked the nobles, made them restore land and stop interest, and himself declined the governor's food allowance for twelve years.

events.title: Resists intrigue and intimidation
events.summary: He refused repeated invitations to meet in the plain of Ono, answering that he was doing a great work, and would not hide in the temple when a hired prophet urged him to.

events.title: Wall completed in fifty-two days
events.summary: Finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul; the surrounding nations perceived that the work had been done with God's help.

events.title: Covenant renewal and dedication of the wall
events.summary: He headed the sealed covenant and organised two great choirs that processed on the wall in opposite directions, with rejoicing heard far away.

events.title: Returns to the king and comes back
events.summary: In Artaxerxes' thirty-second year he went back to the king, then later obtained leave to return to Jerusalem.

events.title: Second-term reforms
events.summary: He threw Tobiah's goods out of a temple chamber, restored Levites' portions, shut the gates on the Sabbath to traders, and confronted mixed marriages, pulling out the hair of offenders and expelling a son-in-law of Sanballat from the high priest's family.

journey.note: Serving as cupbearer at the winter palace.
Travels with royal letters and an escort of officers and horsemen.
Returns to the king's court.
Second term as governor; renewed reforms.

summary:
Nehemiah son of Hacaliah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I at Susa, a position of high trust. In 445 BC news that Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins drove him to months of prayer and then to a bold request: to be sent to rebuild the city. Appointed governor of Judah, he surveyed the walls by night, mobilised the population by families and guilds, and completed the circuit in fifty-two days despite ridicule, threats and plots from neighbouring officials, Sanballat of Samaria, Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arab.

His memoir, written in the first person and punctuated by short prayers ('Remember me, O my God, for good'), reveals a practical, energetic and sometimes fiery leader. He tackled social injustice among Jews themselves, cancelling exploitative debts and refusing his own allowance. With Ezra he presided over the public reading of the Law and a renewed covenant, and he dedicated the wall with two processing choirs.

After returning to court in 433 BC he came back to find abuses reappearing, and dealt with them forcefully. He stands as the Bible's clearest example of a lay leader whose work in government and building is presented as service to God.
textSays: He was son of Hacaliah (Neh 1:1), cupbearer to the king (Neh 1:11), appointed governor (Neh 5:14; Neh 8:9; Neh 12:26), and served twelve years before returning to the king (Neh 5:14; Neh 13:6). The memoir includes his prayers (Neh 1:5-11; Neh 4:4-5; Neh 5:19; Neh 6:9; Neh 13:14; Neh 13:22; Neh 13:29; Neh 13:31).

interpretations.view: Ezra-Nehemiah is counted as one book. The Talmud criticises Nehemiah mildly for speaking of his own merits ('Remember me') and for disparaging earlier governors (b. Sanhedrin 93b), while honouring his work.

2 Maccabees credits him with rekindling the altar fire from hidden thick liquid and with founding a library of the books of kings and prophets (2 Macc 1:18-36; 2 Macc 2:13). He is called 2 Esdras in older Greek and Latin numbering.

Frequently studied as a model of godly leadership: prayer joined to planning, vision-casting, delegation and perseverance under opposition. Some caution against reducing the book to management principles.

The first-person 'Nehemiah Memoir' (largely Neh 1-7 and 13) is widely regarded as an authentic source, perhaps modelled on royal dedicatory inscriptions. Debated points include its relation to Ezra and how the book's editor arranged Neh 8-10.

strengths: Prayerful and decisive
Integrity with public funds
Courage under intimidation
Compassion for the exploited poor
failures: Harsh, even violent, measures in his second term (Neh 13:25)
Some read his repeated 'remember me' as self-regard

context: The Elephantine papyri of 407 BC name Sanballat as governor of Samaria and Johanan as high priest in Jerusalem, confirming Nehemiah's contemporaries. A silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta names Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, plausibly the son of Geshem the Arab. Excavations in the City of David have uncovered fortification lines that some associate with his wall, though the dating is contested.
legacy: Nehemiah gave Jerusalem secure walls and a renewed civic and religious identity that made the Second Temple community viable. Ben Sira praises him for raising the walls and setting up gates and bars (Sirach 49:13).

traditions.text: Nehemiah recovered the sacred fire hidden by priests before the exile, which appeared as a thick liquid and ignited the sacrifice.
Nehemiah founded a library collecting the books about the kings and prophets, the writings of David and royal letters.

voice: Brisk, practical and plain-spoken, with flashes of temper; mixes logistics with quick, one-line prayers and is quick to answer critics with 'I am doing a great work and cannot come down.'

alternatives.label: Some date his return to c. 522-520 BC under Darius I

events.title: Leads returnees from Babylon
events.summary: He heads the list of leaders who returned from exile.

events.title: Rebuilds the altar and lays the temple foundation
events.summary: With Jeshua the priest he rebuilt the altar, kept the feast of Booths and laid the foundation; the old wept and the young shouted.

events.title: Refuses help and faces opposition
events.summary: He declined the neighbouring peoples' offer to help build; they discouraged the work until the reign of Darius.

events.title: Resumes building at Haggai's word
events.summary: Stirred by Haggai and Zechariah, he and Joshua restarted work on the temple.

events.title: Promised the signet ring and 'not by might'
events.summary: Haggai calls him God's chosen signet ring; Zechariah promises that he who laid the foundation will finish it, not by might nor power but by God's Spirit.

summary: Zerubbabel, grandson of King Jehoiachin, was the Davidic governor of Judah who led returning exiles and, with the high priest Joshua, rebuilt the altar and the temple. Halted by opposition, the work resumed in 520 BC under the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, who attached messianic hopes to him. The temple was completed in 515 BC, but Zerubbabel then disappears from the record.
textSays: He is called son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Hag 1:1) but son of Pedaiah in 1 Chr 3:19, perhaps through levirate marriage or adoption. He is governor of Judah (Hag 1:14), God's signet ring (Hag 2:23), and appears in both genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:12-13; Luke 3:27).

interpretations.view: Seen as a token that the Davidic line survived exile; Christians see the hopes attached to him fulfilled in Jesus, his descendant.

Debate continues over his relation to Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:8; Ezra 5:14-16), whether the two are the same person or successive leaders, and whether his disappearance reflects Persian suspicion of royal ambitions.

context: Darius I's accession (522 BC) was marked by revolts across the empire, a background to Haggai's oracles of shaken kingdoms (Hag 2:21-22).
legacy: His temple, later expanded by Herod, stood until AD 70.

traditions.text: As a young guard of Darius, Zerubbabel won a contest of wisdom by arguing that truth is strongest of all, and was rewarded with permission to rebuild Jerusalem.

voice: Steady and conscientious, a builder who speaks of foundations and timber; aware of royal lineage but cautious and deferential to prophetic word.

events.title: Rebuilds the altar and temple with Zerubbabel
events.summary: With Zerubbabel he restored sacrifice and led the rebuilding of the temple.

events.title: Cleansed in Zechariah's vision and crowned as a sign
events.summary: Zechariah saw him in filthy garments accused by Satan, then clothed in clean robes, and later crowned him as a sign of 'the Branch' who would build the temple.

summary: Joshua (Jeshua) son of Jehozadak was the first high priest after the exile, leading the restoration of worship alongside the governor Zerubbabel. In Zechariah's visions he represents the cleansed priesthood and a sign of the coming Branch.
textSays: His father Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chr 6:15); he is named in Ezra 3:2, Hag 1:1 and Zech 3:1-10; Zech 6:11 has him crowned.
legacy: His name is the Hebrew form behind 'Jesus', and Christian interpreters have long read Zech 6:12-13, a priest crowned as the Branch, as pointing to Christ as priest-king (Heb 7:1-17 develops a related theme).
voice: Solemn and liturgical, conscious of the weight of restoring the priesthood.

alternatives.label: If ministry ended before Samaria's fall

skills.name: Poetic imagery of marriage, parenthood and agriculture

gifts.name: Prophecy through his own family life

events.title: Marries Gomer
events.summary: Commanded to take 'a wife of whoredom', he married Gomer daughter of Diblaim as a picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to the LORD.

events.title: Gives his children prophetic names
events.summary: His children were named Jezreel (judgment on Jehu's house), Lo-ruhamah ('not pitied') and Lo-ammi ('not my people').

events.title: Buys back an adulterous wife
events.summary: Told to love again a woman loved by another, he bought her for silver and barley and required a period of faithfulness, a sign of Israel's future return to the LORD and to David their king.

events.title: Pleads with Ephraim
events.summary: His oracles portray God as a parent who taught Ephraim to walk and whose compassion is kindled, closing with a call to return and a promise of healing.

summary: Hosea son of Beeri prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last decades, from the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II to the eve of Samaria's fall. Commanded to marry Gomer and later to redeem an adulterous wife, he made his own marriage a living parable of God's wounded, persistent love for faithless Israel. His book joins sharp indictments of Baal worship, political intrigue and empty ritual with some of the tenderest language about God in the Old Testament.
textSays: The superscription dates him to Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel (Hos 1:1). Jesus twice quotes 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matt 9:13; Matt 12:7; Hos 6:6); Matthew applies 'out of Egypt have I called my son' to Jesus (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1); Paul applies the renaming of 'not my people' to gentile believers (Rom 9:25-26).

interpretations.tradition: Literal reading (many modern commentators, ancient and modern)
interpretations.view: Hosea actually married a promiscuous woman, or a woman who later became unfaithful (the description being proleptic), and chapter 3 describes his reconciliation with Gomer.

interpretations.tradition: Visionary or allegorical reading (Ibn Ezra, Maimonides, Calvin and others)
interpretations.view: Because a literal command to marry a harlot seemed morally problematic, the marriage was understood as a prophetic vision or parable rather than an actual event (Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* 2.46).

Some scholars critique the marriage metaphor's portrayal of female sexuality and divine violence (Hos 2:3-10), while others argue the metaphor's aim is to shame male elites and to culminate in restoration.

context: Israel was wealthy under Jeroboam II but descended into rapid coups after his death (2 Kgs 15:8-30), alternately courting Assyria and Egypt (Hos 7:11), until Samaria fell in 722 BC.
legacy: Hosea's portrait of covenant as marriage shaped later prophets (Jer 3; Ezek 16) and the New Testament image of Christ and the church as bridegroom and bride.
voice: Anguished and lyrical, shifting abruptly between accusation and tenderness, speaking of God as a betrayed husband and a heartbroken parent.

alternatives.label: Early date: minority of Joash of Judah

events.title: Calls Judah to repent after a locust plague
events.summary: He interpreted a devastating locust invasion as a forerunner of the day of the LORD and called priests and people to fast and 'rend your heart, and not your garments'.

events.title: Promises the outpouring of the Spirit
events.summary: God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters would prophesy, and whoever calls on the name of the LORD would be delivered.

summary: Joel son of Pethuel is known only from his short book, which turns a locust plague into a summons to repentance and a vision of the day of the LORD. His promise of the Spirit poured out on all flesh was quoted by Peter at Pentecost as fulfilled.
textSays: The book gives no date. Peter cites Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21) and Paul cites Joel 2:32 (Rom 10:13).

interpretations.view: Early dating points to its place among eighth-century books and the absence of a king; late dating (most critical scholars) points to the temple's existence with no king, mention of Greeks (Joel 3:6), and dependence on other prophets.
Pentecost is read as the inauguration of Joel's promise; interpreters differ on whether the cosmic signs are already fulfilled or still future.

voice: Urgent and liturgical, blowing the trumpet in Zion and summoning everyone from elders to infants to the solemn assembly.

events.title: Oracles against the nations, ending with Israel
events.summary: He condemned the atrocities of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab and Judah, then turned the same formula on Israel for selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.

events.title: Denounces luxury and empty worship
events.summary: He called Samaria's wealthy women 'cows of Bashan' and declared that God hated their feasts: 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream'.

events.title: Five visions of judgment
events.summary: He interceded successfully after visions of locusts and fire, but the plumb line, the basket of summer fruit and the Lord at the altar announced judgment that would not be turned back.

events.title: Expelled from Bethel by Amaziah
events.summary: The priest of Bethel reported him to Jeroboam and told him to go back to Judah. Amos replied he was no prophet nor a prophet's son but a herdsman whom the LORD had taken from following the flock.

events.title: Promises the rebuilt booth of David
events.summary: His book closes with the fallen tabernacle of David raised up and Israel replanted in its land; James cites this at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16-17).

journey.note: Home village in the Judean hills south of Bethlehem.
Preaches at the royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom.

summary: Amos was a herdsman and tender of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah who was sent north to prophesy in Israel during the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, 'two years before the earthquake'. In blunt, artful speech he denounced the exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts and luxurious religion, announcing that the day of the LORD would be darkness for Israel. He is the earliest of the writing prophets and the classic voice of biblical social justice.
textSays: He dates his words to Uzziah and Jeroboam II, two years before the earthquake (Amos 1:1), describes his background (Amos 7:14-15), and records his confrontation at Bethel (Amos 7:10-17). Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 (Acts 7:42-43).

interpretations.view: Read as the prophet of justice whose call for righteousness to roll like a river (Amos 5:24) was famously echoed by Martin Luther King Jr.
Many regard the hopeful ending (Amos 9:11-15) and the oracle against Judah as later additions; others defend their originality as part of the book's design.

context: Excavations at Hazor and other sites show destruction layers attributed to a major earthquake around 760 BC. Ivory inlays found at Samaria illustrate his 'beds of ivory' (Amos 6:4).
legacy: Amos made social ethics central to prophetic religion and supplied the phrase 'a famine of hearing the words of the LORD' (Amos 8:11).
voice: Blunt, rural and unflinching, drawing images from lions, snares, harvest and plumb lines; refuses professional credentials and speaks as one compelled.

events.title: Oracle against Edom
events.summary: He announced that proud Edom, secure in its rocky heights, would be brought down for standing aloof and gloating when Jerusalem was plundered, and that the kingdom would be the LORD's.

summary: Obadiah is the author of the shortest book of the Old Testament, a single oracle condemning Edom for betraying Judah on the day of Jerusalem's calamity. Nothing else is known of him; most date the book soon after 586 BC, though some place it in the ninth century.
textSays: The book gives only his name (Obad 1:1). Its charges (Obad 1:10-14) closely parallel Jer 49:7-22 and Ps 137:7.

traditions.text: The prophet Obadiah was the same as Ahab's steward Obadiah who hid a hundred prophets, and was an Edomite convert.

voice: Terse and fierce, speaking with poetic indignation at a brother nation's betrayal.

alternatives.label: Any point in Jeroboam II's reign

events.title: Prophesies Israel's expansion under Jeroboam II
events.summary: Jonah son of Amittai from Gath-hepher foretold that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's border from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah.

events.title: Called to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish
events.summary: Told to cry against Nineveh, he went down to Joppa, paid the fare, and boarded a ship heading for Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

events.title: The storm and the sailors
events.summary: A great storm struck; while the pagan sailors prayed, Jonah slept. The lot fell on him; he confessed that he feared the LORD who made sea and land and told them to throw him overboard. The sea calmed and the sailors feared the LORD and sacrificed.

events.title: Swallowed by a great fish
events.summary: The LORD appointed a great fish to swallow him, and he was inside it three days and three nights.

events.title: Prayer from the belly of the fish
events.summary: He prayed a psalm of thanksgiving for rescue from the deep, ending 'Salvation is of the LORD'; the fish vomited him onto dry land.

events.title: Second commission and preaching in Nineveh
events.summary: Sent again, he walked a day's journey into the great city proclaiming 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown'.

events.title: Nineveh repents and is spared
events.summary: The people believed God; the king put on sackcloth and decreed a fast even for animals. God saw their turning and relented from the disaster.

events.title: Angry at God's mercy
events.summary: Jonah was furious, explaining that he had fled because he knew God was gracious, merciful and slow to anger, and asked to die.

events.title: The plant, the worm and God's question
events.summary: Sitting east of the city, he rejoiced over a plant that shaded him, then grieved when a worm killed it. God asked whether he should not pity Nineveh, with more than 120,000 people and much livestock. The book ends on the question.

journey.note: Goes down from the hill country to the port to escape his commission. His home was Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kgs 14:25).
Intended destination at the far west of the known world; never reached, as he was thrown into the sea en route.
After being cast up on land, travels to the Assyrian city and preaches; ends sitting east of it.

summary:
Jonah son of Amittai, from Gath-hepher in Galilee, was a prophet of the northern kingdom who correctly foretold Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders. The book bearing his name, however, tells of a very different mission: he was sent to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, Israel's most feared enemy, and he ran the other way. A storm, a great fish, and a prayer from the deep brought him back; a single short sentence of warning then produced the repentance of the entire city, from king to cattle.

Unlike other prophetic books, Jonah is almost entirely narrative, and its sharpest irony falls on the prophet himself. Pagan sailors and Ninevites respond to God more readily than he does. Jonah's anger is not that his prophecy might fail but that God is exactly as merciful as Israel's creed declared (Exod 34:6). The book ends with God's unanswered question about his compassion for a city of foreigners and animals.

Jesus used 'the sign of Jonah' to speak of his own death and resurrection and to rebuke his generation, saying the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment because they repented at Jonah's preaching. Whether the book records history or is a didactic story is debated, but all readings agree on its theme: the breadth of God's mercy and the narrowness of the human heart.
textSays: 2 Kgs 14:25 names him as son of Amittai from Gath-hepher in the days of Jeroboam II. The book narrates his flight (Jonah 1:1-3), the storm (Jonah 1:4-16), the fish (Jonah 1:17), his prayer (Jonah 2:1-9), his preaching (Jonah 3:1-4), Nineveh's repentance (Jonah 3:5-10), and his anger (Jonah 4:1-11). Jesus speaks of the sign of the prophet Jonah, his three days in the belly of the fish, and the Ninevites' repentance (Matt 12:38-41; Matt 16:4; Luke 11:29-32).

interpretations.view: The book is read in full at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur as a lesson in repentance and God's readiness to forgive. Some rabbinic interpreters explain Jonah's flight as zeal for Israel, fearing that gentile repentance would shame unrepentant Israel (Mekhilta, Pisha 1).

Jonah is a type of Christ's death, burial and resurrection; the image of Jonah cast up by the fish is one of the most common scenes in early Christian catacomb art. His story also prefigures the gospel going to the gentiles.

The book is historical narrative: Jesus treats Jonah and the Ninevites' repentance as real events alongside the queen of the South, and 2 Kgs 14:25 anchors Jonah in history. The fish is a miracle, not a natural event.

The book is often read as a didactic narrative or satirical parable, probably post-exilic (5th-4th century BC) on grounds of language and theme, using a known prophet as its protagonist to challenge narrow nationalism. Proponents argue that Jesus can cite a story's characters as one cites a parable; critics reply that Jesus' argument assumes real repentance.

strengths: Honest about his own failure
Willing to be thrown overboard to save the sailors
Composes a psalm of trust in distress
Obeys the second commission
failures: Cares more for a plant than for a city

context: Nineveh became Assyria's capital under Sennacherib (c. 700 BC) but was a major city long before. Assyria experienced internal weakness, revolts, plague and a solar eclipse (763 BC) in the first half of the eighth century, which some propose as a background for the city's openness to Jonah's message. The 'king of Nineveh' (Jonah 3:6) is an unusual title, discussed in the dating debate.
legacy: Jonah became shorthand for a reluctant prophet and for an unlucky passenger. The book's question about God's compassion for outsiders made it a key text for Christian mission and for Jewish reflection on repentance. The Hebrew 'great fish' was rendered *ketos* (sea monster) in Greek (Matt 12:40), later popularly 'whale'. Augustine and Jerome corresponded over Jerome's translation of the plant as ivy rather than gourd, a change that reportedly caused an uproar in a North African congregation.

traditions.text: Jonah was the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah raised from the dead.
traditions.source: Lives of the Prophets 10 (Jonah); Jerome, *Commentary on Jonah*, prologue

traditions.text: Jonah's tomb is at Nebi Yunus in Mosul, opposite the ruins of Nineveh; the shrine was destroyed in 2014.
Jonah is honoured as a prophet in Islam (Yunus), the subject of Surah 10.

voice: Candid to the point of sulking, quick to argue with God and to quote creeds back at him; when cornered he speaks with startling honesty and fatalism.

events.title: Announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem
events.summary: He announced that Samaria would become a heap and that the wound had reached the gate of Jerusalem.

events.title: Condemns land-grabbing and corrupt leaders
events.summary: He denounced those who seize fields and houses, rulers who 'eat the flesh' of the people, and prophets who preach for pay, declaring that Zion would be ploughed like a field.

events.title: His warning moves Hezekiah to repent
events.summary: A century later elders recalled that Hezekiah heeded Micah's prophecy against Zion and the LORD relented, using it to save Jeremiah's life.

events.title: Foretells a ruler from Bethlehem
events.summary: From little Bethlehem Ephratah would come a ruler whose origins are from of old, who would shepherd in the strength of the LORD; the scribes cite this to Herod (Matt 2:5-6).

events.title: Summarises what the LORD requires
events.summary: Not thousands of rams or a firstborn, but to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God.

summary: Micah of Moresheth, a town in the Judean lowlands, prophesied under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, a contemporary of Isaiah. A champion of rural people dispossessed by Jerusalem's elites, he predicted the fall of both Samaria and Jerusalem, yet also the exaltation of Zion, a ruler from Bethlehem, and God's delight in steadfast love. His words were remembered as having moved King Hezekiah to repentance.
textSays: He is from Moresheth and active under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Mic 1:1; Jer 26:18). Mic 4:1-3 closely parallels Isa 2:2-4. Jesus echoes Mic 7:6 (Matt 10:35-36).

interpretations.view: Mic 6:8 is cited in the Talmud as one of the summaries of all the commandments (b. Makkot 24a).
Mic 5:2 is read as a prophecy of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem and of the pre-existence of the Messiah ('whose goings forth have been from of old').
Many attribute chapters 1-3 to Micah and see chapters 4-7 as including exilic and post-exilic additions; others defend wider authenticity.

context: Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722 BC and ravaged the Shephelah, including Lachish near Micah's home, in 701 BC (Mic 1:13).
legacy: Mic 6:8 is among the most quoted verses on ethics in Scripture, and 'swords into plowshares' (Mic 4:3) became a universal image of peace.
voice: Indignant and plainspoken, a countryman's voice against city elites, full of wordplay and ending in wonder: 'Who is a God like unto thee?'

events.title: Announces the fall of Nineveh
events.summary: He proclaimed that the LORD, slow to anger but great in power, would bring Assyria's bloody capital to ruin, as Thebes had fallen, bringing good tidings of peace to Judah.

summary: Nahum the Elkoshite is known only from his book, a poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh. Written after the Assyrian sack of Thebes (663 BC, Nah 3:8-10) and before Nineveh's destruction by Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, it is the counterpart of Jonah: the same city, now beyond repentance.
textSays: The book calls itself 'the burden of Nineveh' and 'the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite' (Nah 1:1). Nah 1:15 echoes the messenger who brings good tidings (Isa 52:7).

traditions.text: Elkosh is identified variously with a village in Galilee, with Alqosh in northern Iraq (where a tomb of Nahum is venerated), and with a site in Judah.
traditions.source: Jerome, *Commentary on Nahum*, prologue; Lives of the Prophets 11

voice: Exultant and graphic, rushing from image to image of chariots and flames with grim satisfaction at a tyrant's downfall.

names.meaning: Embrace (possibly from an Akkadian plant name)

events.title: Complains of injustice in Judah
events.summary: He asks how long he must cry 'Violence!' while the law is paralysed and justice perverted.

events.title: God raises up the Chaldeans
events.summary: The answer astonishes him: God is raising the Babylonians, a swift and ruthless nation, as his instrument.

events.title: Second complaint and watch on the tower
events.summary: He protests that a holy God should use the more wicked to punish the less wicked, then stations himself to wait for a reply.

events.title: 'The just shall live by his faith'
events.summary: He is told to write the vision plainly; the proud will not endure but the righteous will live by faithfulness, followed by five woes on the oppressor.

events.title: Prayer of trembling trust
events.summary: He recalls God's ancient march in power and resolves: though the fig tree fails and the fields yield nothing, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation.

summary: Habakkuk prophesied in Judah around the rise of Babylon. Rather than speaking to the people, his book records his arguments with God about injustice and the use of a cruel empire as God's tool. The answer, 'the just shall live by his faith', became one of the most influential verses in Christian history, and his closing psalm is a classic expression of joy in God when all else fails.
textSays: He is called 'the prophet' (Hab 1:1; Hab 3:1) and his psalm carries musical terms (Hab 3:1; Hab 3:19). Paul quotes Hab 2:4 (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11), as does Hebrews (Heb 10:37-38), and Paul cites Hab 1:5 in Antioch (Acts 13:41).

interpretations.view: The Talmud says the 613 commandments were reduced by Habakkuk to one principle: the righteous shall live by his faith (b. Makkot 24a). The Qumran Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab) applied his words to the Teacher of Righteousness and the Kittim.
Hab 2:4 as used by Paul was central to Luther's discovery of justification by faith.
The Greek additions to Daniel tell of Habakkuk being carried by an angel to feed Daniel in the lions' den; Hab 3 is used as a liturgical canticle.

context: Babylon's victory at Carchemish (605 BC) made it the new superpower; the book probably reflects the years around Jehoiakim's reign.
legacy: His dialogue form gave Scripture a model for honest questioning of God, and Hab 2:4 shaped Pauline and Reformation theology.

traditions.text: An angel carried Habakkuk by the hair from Judea to Babylon to bring food to Daniel in the lions' den.
traditions.source: Bel and the Dragon 33-39 (Greek additions to Daniel)

voice: Searching and argumentative, voicing hard questions directly to God, then patient on his watchtower, and finally lyrical in trust.

events.title: Proclaims the great day of the LORD
events.summary: He described the coming day as a day of wrath, trouble, darkness and trumpet blast against fortified cities.

events.title: Promises a humble remnant and God's song
events.summary: God would leave a humble, lowly people; he would rejoice over Zion with singing and gather the outcast.

summary: Zephaniah prophesied in the days of Josiah, probably before the reform of 622 BC, condemning Baal worship, astral cults and complacency in Jerusalem. His superscription traces his ancestry four generations to a 'Hizkiah', possibly King Hezekiah, which would make him a member of the royal family.
textSays: He is son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hizkiah, in the days of Josiah (Zeph 1:1).

interpretations.view: Whether Hizkiah is King Hezekiah is debated; the unusual four-generation pedigree suggests a notable ancestor, but the text does not call him king.

legacy: His 'day of wrath' (Zeph 1:15, Latin *dies irae*) inspired the medieval hymn *Dies Irae* used in the Requiem Mass.
voice: Severe and sweeping, piling up phrases of judgment, but ending in tender joy at God singing over his people.

events.title: 'Consider your ways'
events.summary: On the first day of the sixth month of Darius' second year, he asked whether it was time to live in panelled houses while the LORD's house lay in ruins, linking drought and poor harvests to neglect.

events.title: Work on the temple resumes
events.summary: Zerubbabel, Joshua and the remnant obeyed, and on the twenty-fourth day work began.

events.title: The latter glory of this house
events.summary: To those who thought the new temple nothing compared with Solomon's, he promised that God would shake heaven and earth and the nations, and the latter glory would be greater than the former.

events.title: Blessing from this day
events.summary: Using a ruling on holiness and uncleanness, he showed that the people's offerings had been unclean, then promised blessing from the day the foundation was laid.

events.title: Zerubbabel the signet ring
events.summary: He announced that God would overthrow kingdoms and make Zerubbabel like a signet ring, for he had chosen him.

summary: Haggai delivered four dated messages over less than four months in 520 BC, urging the returned community to resume rebuilding the temple that had lain unfinished for some sixteen years. His blunt challenge succeeded: within weeks work began, and the temple was completed in 515 BC. He promised that the modest new temple's glory would surpass Solomon's.
textSays: His oracles are precisely dated to Darius' second year (Hag 1:1; Hag 2:1; Hag 2:10; Hag 2:20). Ezra credits him and Zechariah with the success of the building (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14). Hebrews quotes Hag 2:6 (Heb 12:26-27).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition counts Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi as the last prophets, after whom the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel (Tosefta Sotah 13:3).
The greater glory of the latter house is often read as fulfilled when Jesus entered the Second Temple (cf. KJV 'the desire of all nations', Hag 2:7).

context: Darius I had just consolidated power after widespread revolts in 522-521 BC.
legacy: His call to 'consider your ways' became a classic text on priorities.
voice: Brief, practical and pointed, asking sharp questions and repeating 'consider your ways'.

aliases: Zechariah son of Berechiah son of Iddo

alternatives.label: If chapters 9-14 are his and later

events.title: Call to return
events.summary: In the eighth month of Darius' second year he urged: 'Return unto me, and I will return unto you.'

events.title: Eight night visions
events.summary: In one night he saw horsemen among myrtles, horns and craftsmen, a man with a measuring line, the cleansing of Joshua, a lampstand and olive trees, a flying scroll, a woman in a basket, and four chariots.

events.title: Crowns Joshua as a sign of the Branch
events.summary: He made crowns from exiles' silver and gold and set one on Joshua the high priest, announcing the Branch who would build the temple and bear royal honour.

events.title: Answers the question about fasting
events.summary: Asked whether to keep mourning fasts, he called for justice and mercy and promised that fasts would become feasts and many nations would seek the LORD in Jerusalem.

events.title: Oracles of the coming king and the day of the LORD
events.summary: His later oracles foresee a humble king riding on a donkey, mourning for one pierced, and the LORD standing on the Mount of Olives as king over all the earth.

journey.note: Born in exile into the priestly family of Iddo.
Ministry in Jerusalem alongside Haggai.

summary: Zechariah, of the priestly family of Iddo that returned from Babylon, began prophesying in 520 BC, two months after Haggai, to encourage the rebuilding of the temple. His eight night visions present God's renewed choice of Jerusalem, the cleansing of the high priest, and the Spirit-empowered leadership of Zerubbabel and Joshua. The book's second half (chapters 9-14) is the most quoted prophetic section in the Gospels' passion narratives: the king on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one, and the struck shepherd.
textSays: He is son of Berechiah son of Iddo (Zech 1:1), or 'son of Iddo' (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14); Neh 12:16 lists him as head of Iddo's priestly family. The Gospels apply Zech 9:9 (Matt 21:4-5; John 12:14-15), Zech 11:12-13 (Matt 27:9-10), Zech 12:10 (John 19:37) and Zech 13:7 (Matt 26:31).

interpretations.view: Chapters 9-14 are read as detailed messianic prophecy of Jesus' entry, betrayal, crucifixion and return. Matt 23:35's 'Zacharias son of Barachias' slain in the temple is debated: most identify him with Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chr 24:20-22), some with this prophet.

Most distinguish chapters 1-8 (the prophet, 520-518 BC) from 9-14 ('Deutero-Zechariah', undated oracles possibly from the 5th-4th century), noting changes in style and setting; conservative scholars argue for unity.
Counted among the last prophets; Zech 14:9 ('the LORD shall be one, and his name one') concludes the daily Aleinu prayer.

context: His ministry overlaps Haggai's and the temple rebuilding under Darius I.
legacy: His visions influenced Revelation (lampstands and olive trees, Rev 11:4; horsemen, Rev 6:1-8).
voice: Visionary and hopeful, asking his guiding angel 'What are these?', blending priestly concern for purity with sweeping images of nations streaming to Jerusalem.

events.title: Rebukes blemished sacrifices and careless priests
events.summary: He charged priests with offering blind and lame animals they would not dare give the governor, and recalled the covenant with Levi.

events.title: Condemns faithless divorce
events.summary: He rebuked men who broke faith with the wife of their youth and married daughters of a foreign god.

events.title: Announces the messenger and the robbing of God
events.summary: God would send his messenger to prepare the way and come suddenly to his temple as a refiner; the people were robbing God in tithes and offerings.

events.title: Promises Elijah before the day of the LORD
events.summary: The sun of righteousness would rise with healing; Elijah would come to turn the hearts of fathers to children.

summary: Malachi is the last book in the Christian Old Testament. Its prophet, whose name means 'my messenger' and may be a title rather than a personal name, addressed a disillusioned community after the temple was rebuilt, likely in the mid-fifth century BC. Through a series of disputes he confronted shoddy worship, broken marriages and withheld tithes, and promised a coming messenger and the return of Elijah.
textSays: The book gives no genealogy (Mal 1:1). The Gospels identify the messenger of Mal 3:1 with John the Baptist (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10) and Elijah of Mal 4:5-6 with John's role (Matt 11:14; Luke 1:17). Paul quotes Mal 1:2-3 (Rom 9:13).

interpretations.view: The Septuagint renders Mal 1:1 'by the hand of his messenger', and the Targum adds 'whose name is Ezra the scribe'; many scholars treat the book as anonymous, while others accept Malachi as a personal name.
Elijah's promised return is anticipated at every Passover seder with a cup for Elijah.
Its closing prophecy forms a bridge to the Gospels, which open with John the Baptist in the spirit of Elijah.

context: References to a governor (Mal 1:8) and a functioning temple, together with the issues also addressed by Ezra and Nehemiah (mixed marriages, tithes), point to the Persian period after 515 BC.
legacy: In the Christian ordering, his promise of Elijah is the last word before the New Testament.

traditions.text: Malachi was Ezra the scribe.
traditions.source: Targum Jonathan on Mal 1:1; Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 15a (view of R. Joshua ben Korha)

voice: Argumentative and probing, framing God's charges as dialogues ('Yet ye say, Wherein…?'), firm but ending on hope.

names.meaning: Sin (the moon god) has replaced the brothers

events.title: Invades Judah
events.summary: He captured Judah's fortified cities and received heavy tribute from Hezekiah.

events.title: Besieges Lachish and sends the Rabshakeh
events.summary: From Lachish he sent officials to demand Jerusalem's surrender, mocking the LORD as no different from the gods of conquered nations.

events.title: Withdraws after the angel strikes his army
events.summary: The angel of the LORD struck 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, and he returned to Nineveh.

events.title: Assassinated by his sons
events.summary: While worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, he was killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer, and Esarhaddon reigned in his place.

journey.note: Royal capital, which he rebuilt on a grand scale.
Besieges and takes Judah's second city.
Threatens the city through envoys and letters but does not take it.
Returns home.

summary: Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC and rebuilt Nineveh as a magnificent capital. In 701 BC he crushed a western rebellion, devastating Judah and besieging Lachish, but did not take Jerusalem. The Bible attributes his withdrawal to the angel of the LORD; his own annals claim victory and tribute but notably do not claim Jerusalem's capture. He was murdered by his sons twenty years later.
textSays: 2 Kgs 18:13-19:37, 2 Chr 32:1-23 and Isa 36:1-37:38 record his invasion, his officials' speeches and letter, the destruction of his army and his assassination.

interpretations.view: The deliverance is a miraculous act of God in answer to Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's word.

Many accept a historical withdrawal without capture, explaining it variously by plague, an Egyptian relief army (2 Kgs 19:9), or negotiated tribute; some hypothesise two separate campaigns. Herodotus preserves an Egyptian story of mice gnawing the Assyrians' bowstrings (*Histories* 2.141).

context: His annals (Taylor Prism and Oriental Institute Prism) claim forty-six Judean cities taken and Hezekiah shut up 'like a bird in a cage'. The Lachish reliefs from his Nineveh palace, now in the British Museum, depict the siege. Babylonian sources confirm his murder by a son in 681 BC.
legacy: He became an emblem of arrogant power humbled, celebrated in Byron's poem 'The Destruction of Sennacherib'.
voice: Boastful and imperial, listing conquered cities and mocking the gods of other nations.
